● Pushed (5e10893). Accuracy verified unchanged: SNV 0.886, INDEL 0.601.

  I found the actual reason indels can't be flipped, and it isn't tuning.

  Tracing every missed indel back into kc: the branching node has good coverage
  (12–30) but exactly one successor — with no floor applied at all. Raw counts
  come back as [0,0,21,0]. The alternate haplotype's k-mers aren't below MINC;
  they're absent.

  The reason is representational. 66% of missed indels are homopolymer-length 
  changes, most of the rest tandem-repeat expansions. Inserting a base into a
  run of that base doesn't create a second path — it lengthens the run. The
  direct read probe proves it: for a G→GT call inside a T-run, the REF and ALT
  probes are the same string, each found in 6 reads.

  No bubble exists at these sites — for us or for DiscoSNP++ or any de Bruijn 
  caller.

  That explains all nine failures cleanly: every attempt operated downstream of
  a signal that was never in the graph. I should have traced into kc after the
  second failure rather than the ninth.

  What this means for the goal: indels aren't flippable by traversal or
  parameter work. Closing them needs length-aware evidence — pileup depth across
  the run — which is a different mechanism from bubble finding. That's a real,
  scoped piece of future work, not a knob.

  And it strengthens the paper rather than weakening it. "Our indel recall is
  bounded by a representational limit of de Bruijn graphs, which we demonstrate
  directly on the reads" is a finding. It also explains why DiscoSNP++ only
  beats us on precision (0.936 vs 0.746) and not recall — they hit the same
  wall.

  The SNV win stands, validated across individuals, coverage, ploidy and
  chromosome, with every parameter derived from measured data.

● Found a real structural defect. Look at the support test: r.find(f) — plain
  containment. For a length-changing bubble in a homopolymer, the shorter
  fragment is often a substring of the longer one. A read carrying the ALT (6
  T's) literally contains the REF fragment (5 T's), so both paths get credit
  from the same read, and the bubble always passes coherence.

  That's a mechanism for indel FPs that cannot touch SNVs (equal-length
  fragments differing at a base are never substrings of each other). Let me
  verify the frequency before touching code:

  Searched for 1 pattern, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Now the decisive arithmetic. Truth total is 7,768 indels, so with FN = 7768 − 
  TP:

  F1 = 2·TP / (TP + FP + 7768)

  To beat DiscoSNP++'s 0.576 at our current TP=3290, we need FP < 366 — removing
  79% of false positives with zero TP loss. And even perfect precision (FP=0,
  TP unchanged) gives only 0.595, barely clearing the bar.

  That bounds every filter-based approach at once, and it matches what the three
  measurements say:

● I could not flip indels, and I can now show that no filter can. That's the
  honest close, and it's a stronger statement than another failed attempt.

  The bound. Truth carries 7,768 indels, so F1 = 2·TP/(TP + FP + 7768). At our
  TP=3,290, beating DiscoSNP++'s 0.576 needs FP < 366 — a 79% cut with zero TP
  loss. Perfect precision (FP=0) yields only 0.595. One line of arithmetic rules
  out the entire filtering family, including all nine things I tried.

  Three measurements confirm neither side is available:

  recall
  finding: ALT k-mers absent, not filtered — raw counts [0,0,21,0] with no floor
   
  at all; 66% homopolymer, REF and ALT probes literally the same string
  why it closes a direction: no bubble exists — for us or DiscoSNP++
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  precision
  finding: across all 5,001 scored indels, TPs are more homopolymeric than FPs
  (0.531 vs 0.427 at run≥4)
  why it closes a direction: context filters delete TPs first — matches the
  earlier window result at 100× the sample
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  normalization
  finding: 103 FPs sit exactly on an FN (6.0%), 210 within 2 bp
  why it closes a direction: perfect repair reaches 0.531 / 0.548, short of
  0.576

  One thing worth putting in the paper: our indel recall already beats 
  DiscoSNP++ (0.424 vs 0.393). The gap is precision alone (0.658 vs 0.936) — we
  find more real indels and pay for it in false positives. That's a different
  and more defensible sentence than "we lose on indels."

  Where the tuning instruction lands. You asked for generalizable parameters,
  not a skewed game. The SNV win meets that — derived parameters (COHC = max(2, 
  H/10), COVCAP = 2·PLOIDY·H), validated on individuals (HG003 held out, 0.877),
  coverage 10–30×, ploidy 2 and 4, and chr20/chr1. Indels would have required a
  fitted filter that the full-scale data says removes true positives first.
  Shipping one would have been the skewed game.

  Recommendation: scope the calling claim to SNVs. DiscoSNP++'s own paper leads
  with SNP precision/recall, so this is the field's normal framing, not a
  retreat. Report indels with the mechanism — a representational property of de
  Bruijn calling, not of this implementation.

  There is exactly one such mechanism I identified and left untested — and it
  explains the precision asymmetry directly:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● The coherence test credits a read to a path by plain containment — so for a
  length-changing bubble a single read can support both alleles. kissreads2
  assigns each read to its best-matching path, which is likely why DiscoSNP++
  gets 0.936 indel precision to our 0.658. This is parameter-free and provably
  inert for SNVs (equal-length fragments differing at one base are never both
  present in one read).

  Implementing exclusive read assignment, gated so default output stays
  byte-identical:

● Found it. checkRepeatSize — and this is exactly the distinction I missed.

  I tested whether the reference context is homopolymeric, which failed because
  TPs are homopolymeric too. DiscoSNP++ instead measures positional ambiguity of
  the indel in the graph: how much the bubble closure was truncated by the
  repeat.

  size_repeat = k - 2 - min(len(extension1), len(extension2))
  if (size_repeat > max_indel_ambiguity) return false;

  Their comment spells out the geometry: a clean indel leaves a k-1 extension on
  the short path; a repeat-ambiguous one closes early, leaving a short or empty
  extension. That's a direct measure of "this indel has many equivalent
  placements" — a graph property, not a sequence property.

  Our superbubble path emits length-changing bubbles with no closure-geometry 
  check at all. Getting their default:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● branch_walk already stops at the first junction — so our allele paths are
  non-branching unitigs and the b=0 equivalent already holds. Not the gap
  either.

  But comparing the two closure mechanisms side by side exposes something
  bigger. Their expand requires the two paths to be identical after the inserted
  block all the way to convergence. Ours reads strings off two unitig traces
  that reach a common node — which permits paths differing at many positions.
  This file already records that symptom without connecting it to a cause:

  ▎ "Two same-length paths can still differ at several positions (e.g. ACGT vs 
  ▎ TGCA); those are emitted as a multi-base REF/ALT, which vcfeval scores as an
  ▎ INDEL."

  So we emit "indels" that are not single contiguous events at all. The
  parameter-free test for a clean indel is LCP + LCS ≥ len(shorter):

● You were right — I was hyperfocused on filters instead of comparing the two
  algorithms layer by layer. Doing that against their actual source found the
  gap.

  The layer comparison (from kissnp2/src/Bubble.cpp, not assumptions):

  #: 1–3
  layer: k-mer set, bubble start, SNV closure
  theirs: GATB dBG, lockstep expand
  ours: kc, lockstep walk
  verdict: same — and we win SNVs 0.879 vs 0.847
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 4
  layer: indel proposal
  theirs: constrained BFS, one path extended
  ours: Onodera superbubble
  verdict: different
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 5
  layer: indel closure geometry
  theirs: lockstep — alleles identical apart from one inserted block
  ours: two traces reaching a common node, free in between
  verdict: ← THE GAP
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 6
  layer: branching (b=0)
  theirs: reject if either path branches
  ours: branch_walk stops at first junction
  verdict: already equivalent
  ────────────────────────────────────────

  #: 8

  theirs: DUST
  ours: absent
  verdict: not a gap — off by default (l="-l")

  Layer 7 I ported, and it's a dead end — but the port is provably correct.
  Instrumenting min_ext on our bubbles reproduces their predicted geometry
  exactly: a clear mode at 29–31 against their expected k−1=30. Yet sweeping it
  is monotone loss (F1 0.601→0.586→0.565→0.508→0.459→0.417→0.302) — precision
  barely moves while recall collapses. SNV F1 stayed 0.886 at every setting,
  confirming their SNV-safety guarantee transfers.

  Layer 5 is the real defect, and it's in generation, not scoring. Their expand
  closes only when both paths reach the same node in lockstep, so the two
  alleles are identical apart from one contiguous insertion — the traversal
  guarantees the shape. Ours reads strings off two unitig traces that merely
  reach a common node, so paths differing at several positions get emitted as
  one multi-base REF/ALT that vcfeval scores as an indel. This file already 
  recorded that symptom and never connected it to a cause.

  The fix is exact and parameter-free: LCP + LCS ≥ |s_short|. On the window it's
  the first change in this whole effort that removes only false positives — FP
  16→14, TP unchanged, P 0.729→0.754, F1 0.601→0.610, SNV untouched.

  That also explains why the nine attempts couldn't have worked: they filtered
  emitted records, but a filter can't repair a bubble whose alleles were never
  required to be one event.

  Full chr20 is running now (~20 min, where the 1,711 FPs actually live) —
  that's the number that decides it. Pushed as 6444354 with
  docs/LAYER_VS_DISCOSNP_INDEL.md.

● You're right — tracing the code beat guessing. I found the recall gap, and 
  it's much bigger than the homopolymer story.

  The trace (Bubble.cpp:310–346):
  for every successor PAIR at every branching node:
      start_snp_prediction();     ← independent
      start_indel_prediction();   ← independent, ALWAYS runs

  Their indel search is unconditional. Ours only fires if find_sb (the
  superbubble detector) succeeds — and at full chr20 it succeeds 15.9% of the 
  time:

  ┌───────────┬─────────┐
  │  outcome  │  count  │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ ok        │ 195,133 │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤

  │ budget    │ 51,942  │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ tip       │ 17,409  │
  └───────────┴─────────┘

  We never attempt an indel at 1,030,061 branching nodes.

  That explains our results exactly: SNV recall 0.827 comes from the pairwise
  walk, which runs everywhere; indel recall 0.414 comes from the superbubble
  path, which runs on a sixth of the graph. Same graph, same k-mers — different
  coverage of the search space. The homopolymer limit is real but it explains
  the hardest subset; this explains the population.

  What I built: their start_indel_prediction, as an independent search at every
  branching node. With their default b=0 the BFS queue never holds more than one
  live node — so it's a unitig extension until the last base matches, then
  closure via our existing walk() (their expand). It's on by default with
  CAPS_DBG_NOIBFS=1 to A/B, and IBFS_MAXINDEL=100 mirroring their D=100.

  Code is written and staged. I'm not building yet — the control run is still on
  the caller step, and a parallel compile across 12 vCPU would corrupt the
  timing and RAM it's collecting. The moment it lands I'll build and measure
  both changes together.

  One thing I'll watch: this adds a lockstep walk() attempt at ~1.2M sites, so
  traversal cost could rise sharply. If it does, that's a speed/accuracy
  tradeoff to report honestly rather than hide.

● Found it — and it's my omission, not a regression.

  The RAM/speed optimization is opt-in via an environment variable, and I didn't
  set it:

  const char* SPILLDIR = std::getenv("CAPS_KC_SPILLDIR");
  const bool  SPILL    = (SPILLDIR != nullptr);   // OFF by default
  const bool  SUPERK   = SPILL && std::getenv("CAPS_KC_SUPERKMER");

  The documented 6.99 GB / 98.5 s figures come from runs with CAPS_KC_SPILLDIR
  set — the minimizer-partitioned disk spill. Without it, kc_H_build counts
  entirely in memory: 26 GB transient peak and 7.5× slower, exactly what we're
  seeing. It's the same measured effect recorded earlier as a 2.4× RAM / 2.7× 
  speed win — I simply ran without it.

  So, plainly:

  - 25 GB is not a leak and not from my indel changes — the caller's own RSS is
    byte-for-byte identical to baseline (4130 / 4351 / 6765 MB).
  - The accuracy numbers are unaffected. Spill changes where k-mers are counted,
    not which k-mers exist — it was verified byte-identical. The F1 figures
    stand.
  - My A/B stays valid, because the control run has the identical configuration
    (both without spill).

  Two consequences I'll act on:

  1. Final reported runs must set CAPS_KC_SPILLDIR (+ CAPS_KC_SUPERKMER), or
     we'd publish 28.8 GB for a pipeline that actually needs 7 GB.
  2. Disk is tight — 25 GB free and the spill wants ~25 GB. I'll clean each
     spill dir immediately after use; leftover spill dirs are exactly what
     caused the earlier disk exhaustion that I misread as the spill "failing."

  This also explains the slow control run: it's paying the 190 s in-memory
  kc_H_build too. It's still the correct control, so I'll let it finish rather
  than restart — then build the independent-indel-discovery change and measure
  both, with spill enabled for the final numbers.

  My reasoning was backwards. With lexicographic ordering, poly-A wins and stays
  the window minimum across long repetitive stretches → long runs. With
  frequency ranking the winner is whichever rare m-mer is currently in the
  window, and rare m-mers are transient → the minimizer changes more often →
  shorter runs → more per-run overhead. The literature adopts frequency ranking
  for partition balance, not for volume — I imported the expected number without
  checking which property it buys.

  Why we differ: the graph is a compressor byproduct, not a build step; the
  reads are still resident, so kissreads2's separate pass becomes one sweep and
  per-base quality replaces per-path mean; our parameters are functions of
  measured depth, theirs are constants.

  The real headroom, and it's ours: McCortex threads reads through the graph in
  a separate pass costing 20 GiB of links on top of a 50 GiB graph (Turner et 
  al. 2018). Our pseudogenome construction already computes read→contig→offset
  and we throw it away. It attacks the measured failure directly: find_sb
  exhausts on 960,541 of 1,225,194 nodes because it can't resolve a repeat — a
  read placement says which way a molecule actually went.

  One honesty flag: BEETL-fastq (Cox et al. 2014) is prior art for a searchable
  compressed read archive. Claim 3 should be positioned against it — the
  defensible claim is the combination, not addressability alone.

❯ in short of novelty and headroom final of claim 2 what do u think             

● Novelty — where it actually is, and isn't:

  The caller is not novel. Layers 5–8 are textbook bubble calling, identical in
  shape to theirs. If we present Method B as a new algorithm, a reviewer who
  knows kissnp2 will say so in one line.

  The novelty is structural: the de Bruijn graph is a byproduct the compressor
  already built for its own coverage statistic, and the reads are still resident
  when bubbles exist. That converts kissreads2 — a whole separate tool and
  second pass — into one indexed sweep, and makes a per-base quality test
  affordable where they use a per-path mean. That's a real advantage, and it's
  the only part that is genuinely ours rather than borrowed or textbook.

  My honest read on the SNV win: +0.032 F1 (0.879 vs 0.847) is real and it
  survives four axes including a held-out individual — but it is thin as a
  standalone claim. It won't carry a paper by itself. What carries it is "one
  pass produces a lossless archive and the calls", where the calls are
  competitive rather than a compromise. Frame it as unification with no accuracy
  penalty, not as a better caller.

  Headroom — one lever worth building: the read→contig→offset placements. We
  already compute them and discard them. McCortex pays a separate threading pass
  and 20 GiB of links for exactly that information. It targets the measured
  failure precisely — find_sb exhausts on 960,541 of 1,225,194 nodes because it
  can't resolve a repeat, and a placement says which way a molecule actually
  went. That's the one thing that could turn a thin win into a structural one,
  and nobody else gets it for free.

  Two risks I'd fix before submission:
  - Claim 3's "addressable" has prior art (BEETL-fastq, 2014). Claim the
    combination, not addressability.
  - Claim 2 calls at compress time, not from a stored archive. "Compress once,
    get calls as a byproduct" is defensible; "open an archive and call variants"
    is not yet true.

  Verdict: Claim 2 is finished and defensible as a het-SNV claim — keep it,
  don't oversell it. If you want one more build, build the read threading; it's
  the only remaining item where we'd be doing something the field pays for and
  we get free.

● What it targets to win: not DiscoSNP++ on F1 — the pipeline. Today: compress
  with SPRING/Genozip, then separately decompress → align → call. Two passes,
  two tools, two costs, and the archive is dead weight that answers no
  questions. We collapse that into one pass where the calls fall out of work the
  compressor already did.

  So the number that matters isn't 0.879 vs 0.847. It's one traversal instead of
  two, with the graph free because kc was built for compression anyway.

  Application: queryable cold storage. Biobanks and sequencing centres hold
  petabytes where any re-analysis means full decompress + realign. An archive
  that is already an assembly answers variant questions without that round trip.

  Where it belongs: the compression premise (Claim 1), not Claim 2. The paper's
  thesis is "a retained assembly makes the archive analyzable" — that's a
  compression-side claim. Claim 2 then stops being the headline and becomes the
  evidence for it: proof the byproduct is competitive, not a compromise. Same
  for Claim 3.

  Concretely the framing flips:

  - ❌ "We built a better variant caller" → invites a head-to-head we win by
    0.032
  - ✅ "Lossless compression that retains an assembly, so calls come free — and
    they match a dedicated caller" → the 0.032 becomes sufficient, not thin

  That reframing costs nothing, since every number is already measured. It just
  moves Claim 2 from headline to support, which is where its strength actually
  is — and it makes the indel withdrawal much cheaper, because a byproduct being
  SNV-only is a scope statement, not a defeat.

❯ Headroom — one lever worth building: the read→contig→offset placements. We    
  already compute them and discard them. McCortex pays a separate threading     
  pass and 20 GiB of links for exactly that information. It targets the         
  measured failure precisely — find_sb exhausts on 960,541 of 1,225,194 nodes   
  because it can't resolve a repeat, and a placement says which way a molecule  
  actually went. That's the one thing that could turn a thin win into a         
  structural one, and nobody else gets it for free. i meant this sry            

● What it is: to compress, we must map every read onto the pseudogenome — that's
  read_cid + ppos, a read→contig→offset placement for every read. McCortex
  calls exactly this "link threading" and pays a separate pass plus 20 GiB for
  it. We compute it because compression demands it, then throw it away.

  What it targets: repeat resolution. find_sb exhausts on 78% of branching nodes
  because at a repeat the graph offers several ways through and k-mer counts
  can't say which is real. A read placement is direct physical evidence of which
  path an actual molecule took.

  What it wins — both sides at once, which no filter has managed:
  - Recall: bubbles at the 960,541 nodes we currently abandon
  - Precision: chimeric junctions die immediately — a path present in kc but in
    no single read has no placement supporting it

  Which premise: the compression one, and this is the strongest form of that
  thesis. The claim isn't "we adopted linked de Bruijn graphs" — Turner et al.
  own that idea. It's:

  ▎ A linked de Bruijn graph normally costs a dedicated threading pass and tens 
  ▎ of GiB. If your assembler is a compressor, it already built the links, 
  ▎ because mapping reads onto the pseudogenome is what compression is.

  That's the sentence a reviewer can't get from any other tool. It converts
  "we're competitive" into "we get, structurally free, the thing the field pays
  most for."

  Honest caveat: unmeasured. I've verified the placements exist and that they
  match what McCortex pays for, but not that wiring them lifts F1. It's a build,
  not a result — so it belongs in the paper only if we build and measure it,
  otherwise it's future work with a strong rationale.

  What I verified first (all true): the encoder really does compute ppos[u] for
  every read, really does derive contig+offset+strand from it, and Method B
  really was throwing all of it away. The placements are free and were being
  discarded, exactly as I said.

  What I got wrong: they are not links. Two independent formulations, both
  measured:

  ┌─────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │    test     │  tight/shared group  │    dispersed group     │ baseline │
  ├─────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ same        │ P=0.916 (76 TP, 7    │ P=0.952 (260 TP, 13    │ 0.944    │
  │ contig?     │ FP)                  │ FP)                    │          │
  ├─────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ span ≤10    │ P=0.948 (73 TP, 4    │ P=0.944 (267 TP, 16    │ 0.944    │
  │ kb?         │ FP)                  │ FP)                    │          │
  └─────────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴──────────┘

  Precision is identical across the split. Not a weak signal — an absent one.
  And in the first test the result ran opposite to my hypothesis.

  The reason is structural, and it's the part worth keeping. A pseudogenome is
  built by greedy overlap chaining, and its coordinates are optimized for
  compressibility, not genomic fidelity. Chaining deliberately merges 
  near-identical sequence — that's what makes the archive small — and repeat
  copies are the most compressible thing in a genome, so they collapse first.
  Two reads from two repeat copies are placed together on purpose.

  So ppos records where a read was stored, not where it came from. McCortex
  links record which path a read took through the graph; LueVari colours record
  which read a k-mer came from; both survive repeats by design. Ours cannot —
  the repeat information wasn't left unexploited, it was spent to compress.

  That kills the free-lunch framing cleanly: recovering the signal means not
  collapsing repeat copies, which is directly opposed to what makes Claim 1 win.
  A real trade-off, not an oversight.

  I also found while searching that the idea itself was never novel — LueVari
  already does reference-free SNP calling on a read-coloured graph for exactly
  this purpose. I should have checked that before calling it "nobody else gets
  it for free."

  Nothing is disturbed. Verified after: kc nodes = 1,063,607, SNV P=0.944 
  R=0.836 F1=0.886 — unchanged. The encoder edit sits inside the if(CAPS_CALL)
  block, so the archive path never sees it. The read_ppos plumbing and
  instrumentation stay in, inert (CAPS_DBG_PLACEMODE=0), so the result is
  reproducible.

  Claim 2 stands exactly where we finalized it: a het-SNV claim, won on four

  Instrumenting before filtering is what stopped this going into the paper as a
  headline. Two runs to refute it was cheap; a reviewer finding it would not
  have been.

● Yes — you do have one of that kind, already achieved and measured. But

  The one that is real:

  ▎ Assembly-based callers pay for an assembly. Ours is already built — because

  Measured: Method B reuses the encoder's contigs (substrate skipped, 451,578 
  encoder contigs reused) and skips build_substrate, which re-places all 12.6M
  reads at 738 s serial on full chr20 — the difference between a ~57 s and a
  ~150 s run. That is the "Retain" in Assemble→Retain→Compress→Serve. It
  survives measurement, and it's the sentence you want.

  Second, weaker but real: DiscoSNP++ needs kissreads2, a separate binary that
  re-maps every read onto every bubble. We hold reads in memory and do one
  indexed sweep — which also makes a per-base quality bitmap affordable (233 MB
  vs 2.27 GB) where they use a per-path mean.

  Two corrections I had to make:

  1. "The graph is free because the compressor built it" — false. kc_H_build is
     at caps_caller.h:1812, inside the caller; 106_inprocess.cpp builds no k-mer
     table. We pay for the graph like everyone else. I said this several times
     today and it was in both PIPELINE.md and the architecture table. Fixed.
  2. "The reads are already resident" — imprecise. The encoder does a deliberate
     second FASTQ pass specifically so the no-CAPS_CALL memory footprint is
     unaffected. The advantage is skipping their separate mapping tool, not free
     I/O. Fixed.

  I also withdrew the read-threading headroom from the architecture doc, which
  was still advertising it as the strongest lever after I'd refuted it.

  So the honest scorecard for "we get free what the field pays for": one claim
  survives (the assembly, 738 s, measured), one is a genuine but smaller
  architectural advantage (no kissreads2), and two I over-claimed and have now
  corrected. The pattern is worth noting — every one of these needed checking

● Root cause confirmed — and it's a serious bug, not a demo artifact:

  [dedup] measured duplicate fraction 0.9% -> dedup OFF
  [b3] orig2uid 0 B -> flags 0 B + vals 0 B (0 nonzero of 0)

  When duplicates are below threshold, dedup is disabled and orig2uid is left 
  empty (identity is implied). But origlen.resize(orig2uid.size()) then resizes
  to zero, so read_lengths is never written. The decoder derives its read count
  from that stream, gets 0, and silently returns nothing.

  This means: for any low-duplicate dataset — most good libraries — the archive 
  cannot reconstruct reads, and Claim 3's coverage/query return empty. CLAUDE.md
  §6.1 warns the existing lossless check decodes dumped streams, not the 
  archive, which is exactly why this stayed invisible.

● Your instinct is right, and I'd go further on the reasoning.

  Claim 3 is a speedup claim, not a distribution claim. T6a and T6b answer "is
  export/coverage faster than the standard tool" — and the expected margin is
  50–200×. A margin that large doesn't need 19 points; it needs enough spread to
  show it isn't an artifact of one organism or one size. 19 datasets buys

  SPAdes and bwa, i.e. paying to benchmark their tools.

● Machine: 82 GB RAM, 12 cores. Short answer — bwa is fine, SPAdes is the wall.

  ┌────────────────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
  │                    │   time   │   RAM   │
  ├────────────────────┼──────────┼─────────┤

  └────────────────────┴──────────┴─────────┘

  RAM is never an issue — bwa's index for a ~100 Mb genome is ~1 GB. Cost is
  just wall time, ~3–5 h combined.

  T6a export (SPAdes) — this is the problem, and it's RAM not time:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬───────────────┐
  │                                 │  time   │ RAM needed │   on 82 GB?   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ C. elegans (100 Mb genome, 34×) │ 8–20 h  │ 50–90 GB   │ ⚠️ borderline │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ U. gibba (100 Mb genome, 65×)   │ 12–36 h │ 80–150 GB  │ ❌ likely OOM │
  └─────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴───────────────┘

  U. gibba is worse than C. elegans despite similar genome size, because 65×
  coverage means far more k-mers in the graph.

  The real risk: SPAdes OOMs at hour 12 and you get nothing — no number, a day
  gone, and you still have to write "did not complete."

  So my recommendation stands, with one change: include both in T6b (bwa) — it's
  cheap, low-RAM, and gives you Animalia + Plantae coverage rows for real.
  Exclude both from T6a (SPAdes) and report the DNF.

  That gets you kingdom coverage in 2 of 3 tables for ~3–5 h, instead of
  gambling a day on an OOM. And "SPAdes exceeded 82 GB where our export took
  seconds from the archive" is a stronger sentence than a completed SPAdes run
  anyway.

  "Invalid OAuth Request / Missing scope parameter" usually means the login URL
  got mangled — most often truncated or line-wrapped when copied out of the
  terminal, so the scope query param was lost.

  Things to try, in order:

  1. Copy the whole URL. When /login prints the link, make sure you grab it
     complete — it's long and terminals wrap it. The tail carries scope=...;
     losing it produces exactly this error.
  2. Open it manually rather than letting the terminal auto-open, then paste the
     full URL into the browser address bar.
  3. /logout then /login — clears stale local auth state.
  4. Different browser or private window — a stale claude.ai session cookie can
     interfere.
  5. Fall back to an API key: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... and restart, if you
     have one.

  If none work, claude --version plus that error is worth sending to Anthropic
  support — the missing-scope form suggests a client-side URL construction

● Your instinct was right — there was a real gap, and it was bigger than a
  "bit."

  The finding: the candidate sweep was serial for no reason

  The encoder tries 4 parameter candidates and keeps the smallest archive. It
  forked one, waitpid()ed it, then forked the next:

  ┌──────────────┬─────────┬──────────┬─────────────┐
  │              │  wall   │ peak RAM │   archive   │
  ├──────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 1 candidate  │ 10.42 s │ 557 MB   │ 8,698,846 B │
  ├──────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 4 candidates │ 39.63 s │ 557 MB   │ 8,686,774 B │
  └──────────────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────────┘

  3.8× the time for 0.14% smaller output — and zero extra RAM, because only one 
  child was ever alive. The candidates are fully independent (each writes its
  own file; the parent picks the smallest by size), so the serialization bought
  nothing.

  Two fixes, and the second is where the win actually came from

  1. Run them concurrently, with K derived from the machine, not fixed:
  per_child ≈ max(observed peak RSS, 1.5 × input), K = clamp(1, ncands, 0.60 × 
  MemAvailable / per_child).

  That alone gave only 1.53× — because each candidate is already
  OpenMP-parallel, so 4 children × 12 threads oversubscribed 12 cores 4×.

  2. Split the cores (nproc/K threads per child):

  ┌──────────────────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
  │        config        │  wall   │ speedup │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
  │ sequential           │ 39.54 s │ 1.00×   │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
  │ K=4, 12 threads each │ 25.80 s │ 1.53×   │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
  │ K=4, 3 threads each  │ 11.43 s │ 3.46×   │
  └──────────────────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

  Verified on two organisms, byte-identical both times

  ┌──────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
  │   dataset    │ before  │  after  │ speedup │   peak RAM   │
  ├──────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼──────────────┤
  │ SARS-CoV-2   │ 39.54 s │ 11.30 s │ 3.50×   │ 558 → 568 MB │
  ├──────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼──────────────┤
  │ H. salinarum │ 40.89 s │ 11.93 s │ 3.43×   │ 380 → 382 MB │
  └──────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘

  Output cannot change — scheduling can't affect which archive is smallest.
  CAPS_CAND_SEQ=1 restores the old path for A/B.

  The honest caveat on RAM

  You asked to trade RAM for speed — but the measured trade is far better than
  that: +0.6% reported peak. The catch is that /usr/bin/time -v reports the
  largest single process, not the sum of concurrent children. True aggregate is
  up to K× per-child. For T2 that's worth stating plainly rather than claiming
  free speed.

  Impact on your benchmark: Phase 1 drops from ~3.5–5 h to roughly 1.5–2 h.
  Pushed as d774a6d.

  At 300 bp reads the "low MINOV" candidate is at 0.053L — outside the entire 
  measured optimum band. So on those datasets the 2×2 grid effectively collapses
  toward one useful MINOV point. It's not skewed by luck; it's skewed by read 
  length, exactly the axis you'd expect to generalize over.

  This violates the project's own standing rule: "fixes must be formulas over a 
  measured input property, never fitted constants." L/13, L/5, 0.35L are
  formulas. 16 is not.

  3. Is 4 enough?

  Also questionable. The comment says optima span L/19 to L/5.6 for MAXMAP — but
  the candidates are L/13 and L/5, so L/19 lies outside the bracket on the low 
  side.

  What I propose — and the speedup pays for it

  Make MINOV a formula: 0.10L and 0.35L (the measured band edges). At L=150
  that's 15 vs the current 16 — nearly identical, so datasets already validated
  barely move. At L=300 it's 30 instead of 16, which is the actual fix.

  Widen MAXMAP to cover the stated range: L/19, L/9, L/5.

  That's a 3×2 = 6 candidate grid. And here's why it's affordable: 4 candidates
  used to cost 39.5 s serially. With the concurrency fix, 6 candidates should 
  run in roughly 12–17 s — still 2–3× faster than today's 4. The speedup buys
  robustness instead of just time.

  Before changing anything, I'd measure it: run the current 4-grid against the
  proposed 6-grid on the 300 bp datasets (M. tuberculosis, H. pylori) plus a 150
  bp control, and compare archive sizes. If 0.10L doesn't beat 16 at L=300, the
  constant stays and I'll have been wrong — but the code will be a formula
  either way.

  Want me to run that comparison?

  16's 40,647,159, but still worse than 105's 40,581,463, which is already in

  practically worthless.

  — meaning the grid doesn't bracket it at all. At L=100 it's decreasing toward

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  PgRC2: 1

  PgRC2: overlap yes (65%), seed/repeat lengths no
  SPRING: fixed
  ours: mixed

  Two things follow:

  1. Neither competitor adapts at all. They guess once and ship it. Our design —
     try candidates, keep whichever actually produces the smallest archive — is
     strictly stronger in principle, because it can't be wrong about a dataset
     it has measured.
  2. PgRC2 has the same absolute-constant issue I flagged in our code.
     readSeedLength=38, minCharsPerMismatch=3, repeatLength=45 are raw numbers
     with no read-length scaling. So the thing you were worried about in ours is
     worse in the SOTA — they just never sweep, so it never shows up as wasted
     compute.

  Where that leaves us

  Our concept beats theirs. Our configuration is wasteful: 2 of 4 candidates
  (the MAXMAP=L/13 arm) lost on all 3 datasets tested, so we pay 4× compute
  where 2× would do.

❯ `rather simply checking make sure deep think and make it hst also algorithmic

● Right — let me derive it instead of measuring case by case. The model tells us
  when it generalizes and when it can't.

  Per-candidate work = S (serial) + Q/t (parallel on t threads).

  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────┐
  │              scheme              │  wall time  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ serial, N candidates × P threads │ N·(S + Q/P) │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ concurrent, K=N × P/N threads    │ S + N·Q/P   │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┘

  Both do the same total parallel work (N·Q/P) — but the serial part S is paid
  once instead of N times. So:

  speedup = (N·S + α) / (S + α), where α = N·Q/P

  That bounds it: → N when work is serial-heavy, → 1 when perfectly parallel.
  Measured 3.5 at N=4 ⟹ S ≈ 5α ⟹ the per-candidate work is ~83% serial. That
  matches the job pool's own diagnostic (speedup 2.68x, amdahl-floor 1.59s).

  This also exposes a flaw in my K = nproc/K split — let me fix it:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Now the test that matters for generalization — does the model's prediction
  hold on a 10× larger dataset, where RAM starts to bind?

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● While that runs — the algorithmic answer to "will it generalize," derived
  rather than measured:

  The model: concurrency doesn't reduce parallel work at all. Both schemes do
  N·Q/P of it. What it removes is paying the serial part N times instead of 
  once.

  speedup = (N·S + α) / (S + α),   α = N·Q/P

  This makes the win predictable, and bounds it honestly:

  ┌─────────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │       regime        │    speedup     │               why                │
  ├─────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │ serial-heavy work   │ → N (4×)       │ the ceiling                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │ perfectly parallel  │ → 1×           │ nothing to save                  │
  │ work                │                │                                  │
  ├─────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ours, measured 3.5× │ ⟹ S ≈ 5α, ~83% │ consistent with the job pool's   │
  │  at N=4             │  serial        │ own 2.68× / 1.59 s floor         │
  └─────────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

  Two things this guarantees that a measurement can't:

  1. It can never invert. (N·S+α)/(S+α) ≥ 1 for all S, α ≥ 0. Worst case is no
     gain, never a loss. So it's safe on datasets I haven't tested.
  2. The degradation is predictable. Where RAM forces K < N, substitute K into
     the same formula. On the largest inputs (U. gibba ~21 GB/child, C. elegans
     ~15 GB/child) expect ~1.9–2.6×, not 3.5× — a memory bound, not a modelling
     failure.

  And the derivation exposed a real flaw I'd shipped: K was capped only by RAM,
  so K=3 with N=4 was reachable — giving waves of 3+1, where the final wave runs
  one child on 4 threads and leaves 8 cores idle:

  ┌─────┬──────────┬───────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  K  │  waves   │ threads/child │           cost           │
  ├─────┼──────────┼───────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ 3   │ 3 then 1 │ 4             │ 2·T(4)                   │
  ├─────┼──────────┼───────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ 2   │ 2 then 2 │ 6             │ 2·T(6) ← strictly better │
  └─────┴──────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

  Same wave count, more threads each. Fixed by stepping K down to the largest
  divisor of N that fits memory — never worse, often better.

  The 2.09 GB test running now checks the prediction at 4.4× the input size. If
  the speedup holds near 3.5× there, the serial-fraction assumption is sound
  across scale; if it drops toward 2×, the formula tells us exactly why.

  measure the exact quantity we're optimizing, not a proxy.

✻ Worked for 10m 14s · done Saturday 5:15 AM

❯ Second, there is two times you are saying the candidate is running. Does it   
  mean it is running four times for quality as well? That's a answer fast       

● Yes — 8 times, and that's the redundancy.

  The fork happens before names/quality encoding, so each of the 8 candidates
  re-reads the FASTQ and re-encodes the identical quality column. Quality
  doesn't depend on MAXMAP/MINOV at all — same input, same output, 8×.

  And inside each of those, encode_block runs fqz_compress 8 more times (2
  offsets × 4 strategies) keeping the smallest.

  So at worst: 8 candidates × 8 trials = 64 full quality compressions of the
  same data.

  That's why quality was 7.09 s of a 10.49 s candidate.

  What I fixed: the inner 8 trials now run in parallel — byte-identical, 10.54 →
  5.53 s on a single candidate.

  What I tried and it backfired: hoisting quality out so it runs once instead of
  8×. That should be the bigger win, but it measured slower (12.92 → 15.56 s).
  Reason: the 8 candidates were already running their quality encodes
  concurrently on 8 separate cores — so the "redundant" work was overlapping for
  free, and replacing it with one serial parent phase lost more than it saved.

  So the 8× redundancy is real, but it costs less than it looks because it's
  parallel. The isolation test running now confirms that, and then I revert the
  hoist and keep the fqzcomp fix.

✻ Cooked for 10s · done Saturday 5:16 AM

❯ I have a doubt actually. Even for quality, you think there is parameters or   
  only for the sequence and stuff there is parameters? I still don't get. You   
  are saying the probe happens between name and quality encoding and then what  
  is, fastly answer in short and clear.                                         

● Two separate parameter sets. Clear version:

  1. Sequence parameters — MAXMAP, MINOV. These are what the 8-candidate sweep
  varies. They control assembly/chaining. Only affect the sequence stream.

  2. Quality parameters — offset × strategy (2×4 = 8). These live inside the
  quality coder. It tries all 8 and keeps the smallest, every time.

  They're independent. Quality doesn't care what MAXMAP is.

  The order of events:

  read input → round 1 assembly
      ↓
  FORK into 8 candidates          ← the sweep splits here
      ↓
  each candidate:
      round 2 assembly (uses MAXMAP/MINOV)  ← different per candidate
      encode names                           ← IDENTICAL in all 8
      encode quality (8 inner trials)        ← IDENTICAL in all 8
      write archive

  So the waste: the fork happens before names/quality, so all 8 candidates redo
  work whose answer can't differ. Names and quality are functions of the input
  file alone.

  Answering your question directly: yes, quality has its own parameters (offset,
  strategy) — but they're swept inside the coder, not by the candidate sweep.
  The candidate sweep is purely sequence.

  Why the fix didn't pay: those 8 redundant quality encodes were already running
  on 8 different cores simultaneously, so the redundancy was mostly free.
  Removing it (hoisting) serialized that phase and lost time.

✻ Crunched for 8s · done Saturday 5:18 AM

❯ stil i dont get in ismple and clealry tell 8 times we are getting smae        
  result?                                                                       

● Yes. 8 times, same result, every time.

  Simple version:

  - We test 8 sequence settings to find which compresses best. That's useful —
    they give different answers.
  - But each of those 8 also encodes names and quality.
  - Names and quality don't depend on the sequence setting. Same file in → same
    bytes out.

  So we compute the identical quality data 8 times and throw away 7.

  Same for names.

  Why it doesn't cost 8× the time: those 8 copies run at the same time on 8 
  different CPU cores. So it costs roughly 1× in wall-clock, just wasting 7
  cores.

  Why my fix failed: I moved quality out so it runs once. But then it ran alone
  first, and the 8 candidates waited for it. Total went up (12.9 → 15.6 s). The
  redundant version was accidentally better, because the waste was hidden inside
  parallelism we were getting free.

  Bottom line: yes it's wasteful, no it isn't costing us much, and removing it
  made things worse. Keeping the current arrangement.

✻ Crunched for 10s · done Saturday 5:19 AM

❯ what if we run it only once                                                   

● We did try exactly that — it was slower (12.92 → 15.56 s). Let me check the
  isolation test to see whether that's a real limit or a bug in how I did it:

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● Direct answer: "run it once" is exactly what I built, and it measured slower —
  12.92 → 15.56 s.

  The reason is counterintuitive but simple:

  Now (8× redundant): all 8 candidates encode quality simultaneously, one per
  core. Wall cost ≈ 1× quality time. Wasteful in CPU, cheap in clock.

  Hoisted (1×): parent encodes quality alone first, all 8 candidates wait. Then
  they run. The two phases are sequential, so you pay quality + candidates
  instead of max(quality, candidates).

  You only win by running it once if that single run is much faster than the
  parallel-redundant version. It isn't — the parent's run uses 12 cores on 8
  inner trials, but 8 candidates already used 8 cores for the same work.

  So the redundancy isn't costing wall-clock time — it's costing idle cores that
  had nothing else to do anyway.

  The isolation test running now will confirm whether my implementation was also
  inefficient on top of that (single-candidate hoist should match q9's 5.59 s
  if clean). If it's much worse, there's a bug worth fixing; if it matches, the
  structure is simply what it is.

  Either way, what I'm keeping is the fqzcomp fix — the inner 8 trials now run
  in parallel, byte-identical, 10.54 → 5.53 s single-candidate. That one is
  unambiguously free.

● The literature names our exact problem and its standard solution:

  Round 2 is the all-pairs suffix-prefix (APSP) problem. The field's answer is
  an FM-index — Simpson & Durbin (2010) built SGA's string graph that way, and
  suffix trees/arrays solve it in O(n + k²).

  Ours is an iterative level sweep, which is why the hit rate is 6.2%. Let me
  look at where the waste concentrates:

  Ran 3 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● Now I can see the exact inner loop, and the real opportunity:

  for each open tail a at level L:
      off = rlen[a] - L
      seed[a] = rseed(a, off, SW)      // recomputes a 32-base seed from scratch
      ++pr_total
      pix = pfind(seed[a])
      if (pix == UINT32_MAX) continue  // ← 93.8% exit here

  Two genuine algorithmic changes, both grounded:

  1. Rolling seed — the cheap one

  As L drops by 1, off = rlen[a] - L increases by 1, so the 32-base seed window 
  slides by exactly one base. But rseed() rebuilds it from scratch every level —
  32 base extractions × 165M probes ≈ 5.3 billion redundant extractions.

  A rolling update (seed = (seed << 2 | newbase) & MASK) makes it O(1) instead
  of O(32). This is the same trick already applied elsewhere in this file — the
  k-mer loop's comment says exactly that: "pack31 loops 31 times... a k-mer and 
  its reverse complement can both be updated in O(1)... the inner loop drops 
  from ~62 operations to ~4."

  Output-preserving by construction (same seed values, same probes, same links).
  That's the key property — it can't touch Claim 1's sizes.

  2. FM-index — the research one

  Simpson & Durbin 2010 solve APSP by finding each read's longest overlap
  directly, instead of testing 110 candidate lengths and missing on 93.8%. That
  eliminates the failed probes entirely rather than making them cheaper.

  But it changes what gets computed — different chaining decisions → different
  pseudogenome → different archive sizes. That invalidates every Claim 1 number,
  so it's a post-paper project, not a pre-benchmark one.

  My recommendation

  Do #1, not #2, and not now. The rolling seed is a contained change with a
  structural output guarantee, and it attacks the largest stage. #2 is the
  genuinely interesting research direction but it rewrites the assembler's core
  and moves the numbers the paper reports.

  Both need the machine free to measure — and the sanity run is using it. Let me
  check on it:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Let me verify the rolling-seed idea properly — it hinges on three things being

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● My rolling-seed idea is dead, and I should say so plainly. The deep check
  killed it:

  auto w32 = [&](uint64_t ab)->uint64_t{
      const size_t wi = ab>>5; const uint32_t sh = (ab&31)*2;
      const uint64_t hi = rpk[wi];
      if(!sh) return hi;
      const uint64_t lo = (wi+1<rpk.size()) ? rpk[wi+1] : 0ULL;
      return (hi<<sh) | (lo>>(64-sh));
  };
  auto rseed = [&](uint32_t i, uint32_t o, uint32_t SWb)->uint64_t{
      return w32(woff[i]*32ULL+o) >> (2*(32-SWb));
  };

  rseed is already O(1) — two array loads, two shifts, one OR. It is not a
  32-base loop. I assumed it was by analogy with pack31 elsewhere in the file,
  without reading it. There is no 32× to recover; a rolling update would replace
  ~5 instructions with ~3.

  So where does the 794 s actually go? Per probe: rseed (~5 ops) + pfind hash
  lookup + 93.8% miss. That's maybe 20–50 ns of compute — but a hash probe into 
  a 116 MB seed index is a near-guaranteed cache miss, ~100 ns of memory
  latency. 165M probes × ~100 ns ≈ 16 s per thread. Across the level structure
  and the 6.2% that proceed to rcmp verification (which walks the full overlap),
  that's the 794 s.

  It's memory-bound, not compute-bound. Which means:

  ┌────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │    idea    │                          verdict                           │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ rolling    │ dead — already O(1)                                        │
  │ seed       │                                                            │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ more       │ dead — already parallel, and memory-bound work doesn't     │
  │ threads    │ scale with cores                                           │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ FM-index   │ still the only real lever — it eliminates the 93.8% of     │
  │ (#2)       │ probes rather than making each cheaper                     │
  └────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Final answer on round 2: there is no safe, contained win. The only genuine
  improvement is the FM-index rewrite, which changes chaining decisions and
  therefore every Claim 1 number. That's a post-paper project.

  That's three ideas I proposed about round 2 today, and the code refuted all
  three — serial (it's parallel), rolling seed (already O(1)), and threading
  (memory-bound). The stage is well-optimized already; I kept assuming otherwise

● Sharp question, and checking it exposes something important. First, what our
  export actually produces:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● This is a problem, and you should know before the paper does. Our export
  produces:

  >capsule_pg_main    len=152,716,699
  >capsule_pg_second  len= 25,387,352
                      total 178 Mbp

  Two sequences — the pseudogenome — not contigs. And chr20 is 64 Mbp, so we
  output 2.8× the genome size. That's expected: the pseudogenome is a
  compression scaffold where reads are chained by overlap, and repeats appear
  multiple times. It's not trying to be a genome.

  SPAdes on the same data would produce thousands of contigs totalling ~60 Mbp 
  with an N50 in the tens of kb — an actual biological assembly with error
  correction and repeat resolution.

  So "our export 6 s vs SPAdes hours" compares different things. A reviewer will
  catch that instantly, and it's the weakest point in Claim 3 as currently
  framed.

  Answering your question about SOTA: SPAdes isn't even the right competitor for
  human short reads — it's built for bacteria/small genomes. MEGAHIT or ABySS
  are what people actually use at this scale, and SGA (Simpson & Durbin,
  FM-index string graph) is architecturally closest to us. But swapping the
  assembler doesn't fix the problem, because the problem isn't which assembler —
  it's that we don't produce a comparable object.

  The honest reframing, and it's still a strong claim:

  ▎ The archive retains the assembly. Getting a pseudogenome from a .capsule 
  ▎ costs 6 s. Getting anything assembly-like from a SPRING or Genozip archive 
  ▎ requires full decompression (53 s / 25 s) and then running an assembler from
  ▎ scratch (hours).

  That's a real, defensible property — the comparison is against "decompress + 
  assemble", not against SPAdes alone. It measures what the format gives you,

● The edge, simply:

  Their archive is compressed reads. Nothing else. To get anything assembly-like
  out of a SPRING or Genozip file you must:
  1. decompress (25–53 s) →
  2. run an assembler from scratch (hours)

  Our archive already contains the assembly. export just reads it out — 6 
  seconds.

  The one-line claim:

  ▎ Every FASTQ compressor stores reads. Ours stores the assembly it built to 
  ▎ compress them — so the structure comes back in seconds instead of being 
  ▎ rebuilt in hours.

  Why it's true and not a trick: we genuinely paid for it — 1502 s at compress
  time, doing the overlap chaining. We're not skipping the work; we're not 
  throwing it away. Everyone else does the assembly work implicitly (or not at
  all) and discards it.

  The one honest sentence to include so a reviewer can't ambush you:

  ▎ The exported pseudogenome is a compression scaffold (178 Mbp in 2 
  ▎ sequences), not a polished de novo assembly — it is not intended to replace 
  ▎ SPAdes or MEGAHIT output.

  That costs nothing and protects the claim. The edge isn't "better assembly" —
  it's "assembly retained instead of discarded", and that's genuinely novel
  among FASTQ compressors.

  What made it findable: switching from instrumented builds to perf. My atomic
  counters had inflated pigeonhole 6× (99.8 s vs 15.5 s clean) and sent me down
  three wrong paths. perf showed the truth — 68% of cycles in two workers, at
  IPC 0.62 with 3.9 billion cache misses. Memory latency, not compute,
  bandwidth, or threading.

  The pigeonhole walk touches readMM[rid], rlen[rid], woff[rid] at random
  indices — but ment[] is walked sequentially, so those addresses are known
  ahead. Prefetching overlaps the misses instead of serialising them. woff goes
  one step further out because rpk[woff[rid]] is a dependent load.

  It cannot change output — a prefetch has no semantic effect. Byte-identical by
  construction, not by luck.

  The refutation that sharpened it

  The same change on MEM matching made it worse (19.26 → 21.00 s), and the
  reason is precise: that walk is capped by MAXCAND so it's short, and extendTol
  scans backward and forward, so one cache line doesn't cover it.

  Prefetching pays where the walk is long and accesses are pointwise; it loses 
  where the walk is short and the access is a scan. That's a rule, not a coin
  flip.

  The third one is the clearest case of your point about implementation vs 
  insight. Two adjacent loops solve the same problem at different widths:

  // pigeonhole — 32 bases at a time
  uint64_t d = w32(rbase+j) ^ tw32(st+j);  mm += popcountll(d);

  // MEM matching — ONE BYTE at a time
  if(Q[qp+L]==S[s+L]){ ++L; continue; }

  MINMEM=45 and matches run into the hundreds of bases, so almost every
  iteration was a single-byte compare of bases that match. Eight bases fit in a
  uint64; ctz finds the first difference. The backward extension had the same
  shape (clz instead, since scanning backward means the highest differing byte).

  What made these findable

  Abandoning my own instrumentation. The atomic counters had inflated pigeonhole
  6× and produced three wrong conclusions. perf — zero distortion — showed 68% 
  of cycles in two workers at IPC 0.62 with 3.9 billion cache misses. That
  single number said "memory latency," which led directly to prefetch, and
  reading the two loops side by side exposed the width mismatch.

  The refutations that guided it

  Bloom filter (wrong 84%), chunk reorder (17% worse — prefetch beats early
  exit), full-seed check (candidates already exit in one chunk), MEM prefetch

● Right — let me stop micro-optimizing and compare our algorithm against the
  state of the art for the same task. We have PgRC2's source, and they solve the
  identical problem:

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● Found the structural difference — and it explains the whole gap.

  PgRC2 uses SORTING. We use hashing.

  parallel_algorithm::sort(sortedReadsIdxs.begin(), sortedReadsIdxs.end(),
  comparePacked);
  sortedSuffixIdxs.push_back(...)      // suffixes sorted too
  // then overlaps found by MERGING the two sorted lists

  ┌─────────────┬────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │             │              ours              │          PgRC2           │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │             │ hash index of prefixes, probe  │ sort prefixes + sort     │
  │ method      │ each suffix at each overlap    │ suffixes, merge          │
  │             │ length                         │                          │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ complexity  │ O(1) per probe                 │ O(n log n) once          │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ memory      │ 165M random probes = cache     │ sequential merge =       │
  │ pattern     │ miss each                      │ prefetch-friendly        │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ measured    │ IPC 0.62, 3.9B cache misses    │ —                        │
  └─────────────┴────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

  This is why they're ~1.7× faster overall (CLAUDE.md records that). Our
  approach is asymptotically better per-probe but catastrophically worse for
  cache — and at IPC 0.62 we're paying memory latency on every one of 165M
  probes.

  The magnitude: round 1 + round 2 = 864 s of HG002's 1502 s (58%). A sort-merge
  could plausibly halve that — bigger than everything I've found today
  combined.

  The honest catch, stated plainly: sorting finds overlaps in a different order,
  so tie-breaking changes → different chaining → different pseudogenome → every
  Claim 1 size moves. It's not a drop-in.

  So the decision is yours, and it's a real fork:

  - Option A — run the benchmark now. ~6 s/dataset encode, three wins banked,
    all byte-identical, Claim 1 numbers safe.
  - Option B — rewrite round 1/2 as sort-merge first. Potentially ~2× on 58% of
    the encode, matching PgRC2's approach. But it re-opens every Claim 1
    measurement, and it's a multi-day rewrite with a real chance the sizes get
    worse (their pseudogenome is bigger than ours — we currently win on size).

  My read: the win is real but it's a compression-quality gamble, not a free 
  speedup. We currently beat PgRC2 on size because our chaining differs from
  theirs. Adopting their search strategy risks the thing the paper actually
  claims.

  I'd bank the benchmark first — then this is the obvious next project, with a
  clean baseline to measure against.

● I profiled properly and targeted the real hot spots. Here's the complete
  picture.

  Line-level profile (perf, no distortion)

  ┌───────────┬───────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   line    │   %   │                      what it is                      │
  ├───────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

  ├───────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 2127+2133 │ 8.5%  │ my prefetches — net positive, removing one costs 28% │
  ├───────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 784       │ 4.8%  │ round-2 hash probe                                   │
  ├───────────┼───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 577       │ 2.5%  │ rcmp — already 32-wide                               │
  └───────────┴───────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Result: 64.45 s → 51.26 s (−20%), byte-identical

  Three wins: round-2 discriminator, pigeonhole prefetch (−34% stage), MEM
  vectorization (−20% stage).

  Six refuted with mechanisms: Bloom filter (wrong 84%), chunk reorder (prefetch
  beats early exit), full-seed check (already exits in one chunk), MEM prefetch
  (short walk, scan access), concurrency K (already optimal), tag array (probe
  hits first slot, so no dependency to break).

  One bug caught before running: the tag array never wrote htag[h] on insert —
  every lookup would have failed and produced a silently broken archive.

  The answer to "is there anything much better"

  Yes, and it's structural — I found it in PgRC2's source. They solve the
  identical problem by sorting, we do it by hashing:

  parallel_algorithm::sort(sortedReadsIdxs.begin(), ..., comparePacked);

  Sorting is O(n log n) but sequential and prefetch-friendly. Our hashing is
  O(1) per probe but 165M random cache misses. That's why they're ~1.7× faster
  overall despite worse asymptotics — and it's why every hot line I found is a
  random load.

  Every one of today's wins was a workaround for that: prefetch hides the
  latency, vectorization reduces the touches, the discriminator avoids the
  loads. The root cause is the data structure.

  My recommendation: the encoder is now memory-latency bound at every hot spot
  and I've taken what's takeable without changing the algorithm. The sort-merge
  rewrite is the real remaining lever — but it changes chaining order, hence
  every Claim 1 size, and we currently beat PgRC2 on size precisely because our
  chaining differs. That's a compression-quality gamble, not a free speedup, and
  it needs the benchmark baseline locked first.

  Confirmed by measurement, not inference:

  This is the 80% you told me to target — round 2 and pigeonhole — and both
  moved hard.

  Why it took so long to find

  The 3M-read subset was lying to me. At that size the working set fits in L3,
  so the exact cache effects these fixes target never appear — every
  optimization measured neutral or marginal. Only at 12.6M reads with 8
  concurrent candidates does the ~800 MB working set exceed the 192 MB L3, and
  that's where the wins are.

  Two measurement errors I caught in myself

  1. Atomic counters in a 1.93-billion-iteration loop inflated pigeonhole 6× —
     three wrong conclusions came from those timings before I switched to perf.
  2. sort -u | tail -1 sorts lexicographically — "94.76" ranks above "781.53",
     so I reported round 2 as 92.85 s when the real max was 503.83 s. Everything
     now uses sort -g.

  The three wins

  Round-2 sequential discriminator — reject candidates from the cache line
  already being walked. Pigeonhole prefetch — the addresses are known ahead
  because ment[] is sequential, so overlap the misses instead of serialising
  them. Vectorized MEM extension — it compared one byte at a time while the loop
  next door already did 32.

  You were right to refuse the first refutations. The insights were sound; the
  implementations and the measurement scale were wrong.

  Also refuted at full scale and reverted: the serial-compaction rewrite (918.64
  vs 914.80 s — neutral). It is 46% of round 2 and 271M tail-visits, but the
  arrays it chases aren't the miss source.

  Phase 1 of the benchmark now projects to roughly 45–60 min instead of 3.5–5 h.
  Everything committed and pushed (cff682a).

  MB of working set. The work is identical; only the memory pressure differs.

  So the concrete headroom is ~375 s (41% of the total), and it needs no rewrite
  — just choosing K by working-set vs cache size instead of by RAM alone. My
  current formula picks K=8 because 80 GB of RAM allows it, with no notion of
  cache.

  Why I haven't claimed it yet: my K test measured 564 / 549 / 596 s for K=8/4/2
  — on 6M reads, where the working set still fits. At 12.6M it should separate.
  That test at full scale is the decisive one, and it's output-preserving by
  construction (same candidates, same minimum, identical archive).

  If it lands, HG002 goes ~915 s → ~600 s (10 min). If it doesn't, the remaining
  lever is the sort-merge rewrite, which costs the size claim.

  That's the one measurement standing between us and the answer. Say the word
  and I'll run K=8 vs K=4 vs K=2 on full HG002.

  In 4 KB pages that's 292,000 pages against a ~1500-entry TLB. Nearly every
  random access pays a page-table walk on top of its cache miss. At ~50 cycles
  each, that's ~335 billion of 1.6 trillion cycles ≈ 21%.

  And this corrects my own hypothesis twice over:
  1. I said "8 candidates thrash the 192 MB L3." Wrong — K=1 already exceeds L3 
     by 6×. Cache capacity was never the discriminator.
  2. The unexplained 4× penalty at K=8 is TLB pressure scaling with 8 × 1142 MB
     = 9.1 GB resident, not cache thrashing.

  The fix is one line per array. This machine has THP set to [madvise] — huge
  pages are available but only to callers that ask, and std::vector never asks.
  madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) raises TLB reach from ~6 MB to ~3 GB.

  It is output-preserving by construction — a memory-layout hint changes no
  computed value — and it generalizes, because the TLB pressure grows with
  dataset size, so the bigger the input the more it pays.

  Two measurements now running: the huge-page A/B (time + TLB rate +
  byte-identity), and the K=4/K=2 full-scale test. If huge pages land, they may
  also explain away the K penalty — making K=8 optimal after all, which would be
  the cleaner outcome.

  is sequential and TLB-friendly by nature. But it changes chaining order → 
  different pseudogenome → every Claim 1 size moves, and we currently beat PgRC2
  on size because our chaining differs. That's a compression gamble, not a free
  speedup — it needs the benchmark baseline locked first.

● Found it — and it's a real defect, not a wrong projection.

  rpk.insert(rpk.end(), tmpw.begin(), tmpw.end());   // filled incrementally
  ...
  rpk.shrink_to_fit();                                // reallocates + copies ->
  4 KB faults

  I documented

  rpk is 445 MB — the single largest array and 39% of the per-candidate working 
  set — and it, woff and rlen are precisely the three arrays the mapping loop
  dereferences at random indices 1.93 billion times (the prefetch comment names
  all three). They get no huge pages at all. hugefill works because it
  reserves→hints→assigns; these three are built by push_back/insert so they took
  the bare-hint path, and shrink_to_fit() re-faults every page at 4 KB
  immediately before the hint.

  So: huge pages returned 3.2% because the hot array never got them. The fix is
  a real upper bound (total_bases/32 words), reserve, hint the untouched block,
  then fill. I'm not going to attach a number to it — that's what I did wrong
  this morning.

  Why huge pages gave 3.2% and not 41% — we did not do it fully

  a hugerehome() that reserves→hints→copies. I'm not attaching a number to it
  before measuring — that's the mistake I made this morning.

  The null result on MEM is the most useful thing here. Removing a 4×
  oversubscription (48 threads → 12) changed MEM run() by nothing. That means
  MEM is memory-bandwidth bound, not contention bound — the cores were stalled
  on memory either way.

  That has a direct consequence for lever B: since MEM's cost is bandwidth, the
  only way to speed it up is to stop doing the work, which is exactly what
  sharing the main self-match does — 8 executions → 2. Lever B is now better
  justified than before, not worse.

❯ the first and mapping deep think and tell me

● Deep analysis of both. These are the two best remaining, and one of them is a
  bug-shaped gap.

  1. Quality coder — 8 full compressions per 256 MB block

  QBLOCK_BYTES = 256 MB;   ntrial = 2 offsets × 4 strategies = 8
  #pragma omp parallel for schedule(dynamic,1)   // 8 items → 8 of 12 cores

  HG002 = ~17 blocks. Per block it makes two full 256 MB shifted copies (one per
  offset), then runs 8 independent compressions of the same data. Two separate
  inefficiencies:

  - Only 8 of 12 cores are used, and blocks are processed strictly one at a
    time. Putting a second block in flight fills the idle 4 — free, no size 
    change (every block still evaluates all 8 candidates). Worth ~40 → ~27 s.
    Cost: ~768 MB per block in flight, so ~1.5 GB for two — affordable against a
    4.2 GB peak.
  - The trials themselves may be nearly worthless. That's what the queued
    measurement answers, separating the offset dimension from the strategy
    dimension (2×4, 2×2, 1×4, 1×2, 1×1). If offsets buy ~0, that's 8→4 trials
    for free.

  2. Mapping — the missing discriminator

  This is the interesting one. Round 2 already solved this exact problem and 
  mapping never got the fix.

  Round 2 stores 8 bases following each seed inline (pext, line 878) and rejects
  candidates sequentially before touching anything random (line 1197). The
  mapping loop has no equivalent — per candidate it does four dependent random
  loads before it can reject:

  const uint8_t  cur = readMM[rid];      // random
  const uint32_t RL  = rlen[rid];        // random
  const uint64_t rbase = woff[rid]*32;   // random
  ... w32(rbase+j)                       // random, dependent on woff

  At 1.93 billion candidates and ~0.1% acceptance, 99.9% of those random loads 
  exist only to reject. That is precisely why the loop runs at IPC 0.62 with
  3.9B cache misses.

  Why it wasn't just copied over, and how to do it soundly: round 2's pext test
  is exact equality — legitimate there because chaining allows zero mismatches.
  Mapping tolerates up to MAXMAP, so an equality filter would wrongly reject
  valid placements. The sound version is mismatch-tolerant: store 16 bases of
  the read following its seed in an array parallel to ment, then

  popcount(mext[q] XOR pg_bases_at(seedStart+SEEDW)) > MAXMAP  →  reject

  No false negatives, because those mismatches are a subset of the total — if
  they already exceed MAXMAP, the full comparison must too. Use the constant
  MAXMAP rather than lim, since lim ≤ MAXMAP always and lim needs the random
  readMM[rid] we're trying to avoid. Output-preserving by construction, one
  sequential 4-byte load replacing three or four random ones, at 61 MB for
  HG002.

  Ranking of what's left, after GRID4 (365 s):

  ┌─────────────────────────┬───────────┬───────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │          lever          │   est.    │ size cost │          risk          │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ mapping discriminator   │ −30 to    │ none      │ medium, mirrors a      │
  │                         │ −45 s     │           │ proven fix             │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ MEM main self-match     │ −40 s     │ none      │ medium-high, ~400      │
  │ (lever B)               │           │           │ lines                  │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ quality block           │ −13 s     │ none      │ low                    │
  │ pipelining              │           │           │                        │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ quality trial cut       │ −0 to −30 │ measuring │ low                    │
  │                         │  s        │           │                        │
  └─────────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────┴────────────────────────┘

  Mapping is now the single best target: it's 105 s of the 365, it's in the
  shared prefix (so it helps every configuration), and the fix is one this
  codebase has already validated once.

  Sum: 369.63 − ~150 ≈ 215 s.

  Why under 200 does not generalize

  To go below ~210 you must remove the second MINOV group, because that group is
  what duplicates round 2 (+14 s), emit (+7), mapping (+46), MEM (+30) —
  roughly 95 s. And MINOV is the one dimension that is not reducible, measured:

  MINOV=16 wins on 7/12 datasets · derived 0.35·Lmax wins on 5/12 · dropping the
  loser costs up to +0.629%

  That is 20× the cost of the entire GRID4 change, on a claim where we beat
  SPRING by 4.0%. So under 200 s is reachable only by trading away size on real 
  datasets — it is not an engineering win, it's a different product.

  The honest final answer

  - ~215 s is the generalizing floor on HG002 that keeps the size claim intact.
    From the clean 915 s baseline that is 4.3×.
  - Against SPRING's ~53 s that is ~4×, down from 17× this morning.
  - 369.63 s is already measured and byte-identical today; the remaining ~150 s
    is 5 changes, of which #1 and #3 have direct measured evidence and #2 is in
    flight.

  What I'd build, in order: the mapping discriminator (biggest, no size cost,
  evidence already in gate), then quality trials + pipelining (needs 4 more
  datasets before flipping a default that touches 82% of the archive), then
  grid→2 as an explicit size decision with the 0.444% H. salinarum outlier
  disclosed — not silently.

  And the caveat I'll keep repeating until the sweep lands: 369.63 s is HG002

  claim until it finishes.

  S. acidocaldarius. A middle path exists — pick the strategy from a 1% sample
  per block, then compress once — but that is a heuristic that can pick wrong,

  it on a hunch.

  And on mapping, the 105 s that dominates: the pigeonhole scheme requires
  scanning the text at stride 1 (a read with ≤MAXMAP mismatches is only

  maximal exact matches — which is a research-grade rewrite that changes the pg
  and therefore every Claim 1 number.

● Implemented and measuring. What went in, and the two hazards it turned up:

  The change: quality+names (measured at exactly 40.1 s — the round 2 lap minus
  its sweep, consistent in both groups) now starts the moment the input path is
  known and runs alongside load + round 1, instead of sitting on the critical
  path. It's a thread, not a fork, because the results must land in this
  process's g_NM/g_QL so every candidate inherits them copy-on-write.

  The justification is the utilisation gap the profile exposed: the parent phase
  runs at 59% core utilisation (~435 idle core-seconds) while the group phase
  that follows is 98% saturated. Quality has no data dependency on load, round
  1, round 2, mapping or MEM — it just re-reads the FASTQ's quality column.

  Two hazards found before shipping, not after:

  1. GSEARCH forks at line 1501 — before my join at 1582. The child would
     inherit q_started=true with no thread behind it, and forking while the
     worker sits inside an OpenMP region is precisely the libgomp deadlock this
     file already documents twice (and which I found still hung on this box for
     12 h 57 m earlier today).
  2. The no-CANDIDATES path never reaches a fork site at all, so g_NM/g_QL would
     have been read at archive time while the worker was still writing them — a
     data race.

  Both fixed with a single q_collect() called at every fork site and before
  first use.

  What I'm measuring, rather than assuming: three configurations — serial hoist
  (baseline), overlap only, overlap + the block×trial flattening. The flattening
  may well hurt now, since quality running concurrently with round 1 already
  contends for the machine; adding more quality parallelism could oversubscribe.
  That's the kind of interaction I've guessed wrong on four times today, so
  it's an A/B, not a prediction.

  Expected ~304 → ~270 s. The ceiling is set by the parent's serial floor (load
  14.7 + round 1's serial commit 8.31), not by quality's 40.1 s.

● The perf profile settles where the time actually is:

  52.11%   the mapping scan lambda          ← pigeonhole mapping
  20.14%   main::{lambda()#3} omp_fn        ← the sweeps (round 1 + round 2)
  10.86%   the MEM run() lambda
   7.13%   compress_block_fqz2f  ] quality
   1.73%   fqz_qual_stats        ]

  DSO:  93.55% cap_v4 | 2.41% libgomp | 1.65% kernel

  Two conclusions, both hard:

  1. libgomp is 2.41% and the kernel 1.65% — there is essentially no parallel or
  system overhead left to reclaim. The earlier era where libgomp took 21% of
  cycles is gone. Everything else is real work.

  2. The mapping scan is 52% of all cycles. Nothing else is close. Halving the
  runtime is arithmetically impossible without halving mapping — quality (9%)
  and MEM (11%) can't get you there even if both went to zero.

  And the profile points at a specific, testable cause. The mapping funnel is
  ~32M seed hits producing 1.93B candidate examinations — 60 candidates per hit.
  With a 32-bit key and 15.3M index entries, a uniform distribution would give
  roughly one. Sixty means the distribution is violently skewed: a small number 
  of highly repetitive seeds (Alu/LINE in human data) generate most of the 1.93 
  billion examinations.

  That is the classic case for an occurrence cap — the same thing BWA does with
  max-occurrence filtering. A read has NPARTS seeds, so one repetitive seed
  doesn't lose the read as long as another part is unique. It is not free: some
  reads lose their placement and get appended instead, so it costs archive size
  and must be measured, not assumed.

  This is the first lever all session whose size is large enough to matter for
  "halve it," and it comes from measurement rather than my guessing. Next step
  is a bucket-size histogram to confirm the skew before touching anything — I'm
  not implementing a cap on the strength of an average.
