❯ so final headroom to half the 270                                             

● Halving 270 is arithmetically impossible. Here's the closed proof, not an
  opinion:

  mapping wall = 108.57 s  (52% of all cycles)
  270 − 108.57 = 161 s

  Even if mapping cost literally zero, you land at 161 s — above the 135 s 
  target. And mapping can't be zero: the pigeonhole scheme requires probing the
  text at stride 1, or placements are missed and the archive grows.

  The rest offers nothing near the gap:

  ┌────────────────────┬───────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    │ wall  │           why it can't give much           │
  ├────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ mapping            │ 108.6 │ 52% of cycles; capped by algorithm, not    │
  │                    │       │ implementation                             │
  ├────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ MEM                │ 49.0  │ bandwidth-bound — proven by the            │
  │                    │       │ thread-budget null result                  │
  ├────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ round 1 + round 2  │ 59.0  │ 31% / 18% serial commit, order-dependent   │
  │ sweeps             │       │ by design                                  │
  ├────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ load               │ 14.7  │ mostly serial parse + dedup                │
  ├────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ quality            │ 40.1  │ being hidden by the overlap, not removed   │
  └────────────────────┴───────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Real headroom from 270: about 40–50 s, to ~225 s — and all of it hinges on the
  seed-occurrence cap, which changes which reads map and therefore costs 
  archive size. If the bucket histogram shows the skew isn't there, mapping's
  52% is irreducible and ~250 s is the floor.

  So the honest ladder for HG002, end to end:

  915 s  →  304 s  (measured, byte-identical)
         →  ~270 s  (quality overlap, byte-identical 6/6 — timing pending)
         →  ~225 s  (seed cap, costs size, only if the skew is real)

  That's ~3.4×–4.1× total, not the 6.8× that halving twice would imply. I'd
  rather hand you that number now than let you plan against 135.

    exactly as we do. So they eat the same repeat blow-up.

    array with open addressing — ours should be the faster of the two.

  So the 52% is not us being naive; it's what the method costs, and the state of
  the art in this family does it the same way. Let me check the wider
  literature for anything genuinely better:

● Web Search("FASTQ compression pseudogenome read mapping seed occurrence cap
            repetitive minimizer speedup")
  ⎿  Did 1 search in 8s

● Web literature confirms the same picture. Three findings, all consistent with
  what the local source showed:

  1. Occurrence capping is standard — and explicitly costs accuracy. The known
  way to handle repetitive seeds is masking high-frequency minimizers, but "an 
  unfortunate consequence of masking is that minimizer matches are no longer 
  guaranteed and accuracy is reduced in repetitive genomic regions." In our
  setting "reduced accuracy" = reads that fail to map = appended raw = bigger 
  archive. So the lever exists, it's standard practice, and it is not free —
  exactly as I flagged.

  2. Minimizers were already tested here and rejected. This project's own record
  shows frequency-ranked minimizers measured +14% archive and were dropped.
  ORCOM-style minimizer bucketing is the alternative seeding scheme, and it's
  been tried.

  3. The one genuinely different idea is "compressive seeding" — reusing
  intermediate seeding results across similar reads, on the observation that
  "over half of BWT and SAL operations are identical across the entire BWA-MEM 
  seeding process at common sequencing coverage." But that's specific to
  BWT/FM-index seeding, which we don't use; adopting it means replacing the
  whole mapping stage with an FM-index, which changes the pseudogenome and every
  Claim 1 number.

  So the answer to "does PgRC2 or anyone do better": no. PgRC2 does the
  identical thing with a slower data structure (unordered_multimap vs our packed
  array), stride-1 scanning, and no occurrence cap at all — so they eat the
  same repeat blow-up we do. The literature's only lever is the cap, which
  trades archive size for speed.

  That makes the bucket histogram now running the decisive measurement: it tells
  us the exact size/speed curve for caps of 8…4096, so if we take it, we take
  it with numbers rather than on faith.

  Sources:
  - PgRC2: engineering the compression of sequencing reads
  - PgRC: pseudogenome-based read compressor (Bioinformatics)
  - A compressive seeding algorithm in conjunction with reordering-based 
    compression
  - Weighted minimizer sampling improves long read mapping

❯ which decides whether the mapping's 52% of cycles has a lever at all, or      
  whether ~279 s is the floor.                                                  

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Exactly — and the decision rule is mechanical, so there's no room for me to
  talk myself into a result.

  The diagnostic prints, for caps of 8/16/32/64/128/256/1024/4096, two numbers:
  what fraction of index entries survive (the accuracy/size proxy) and what 
  fraction of work survives (Σ b·min(b,C), the speed proxy).

  Lever exists if some cap keeps ~99.9% of entries while cutting work sharply —
  e.g. cap=256 keeping 99.9% of entries but 40% of work. That means a tiny tail
  of repetitive seeds generates most of the 1.93B examinations, the reads
  affected mostly have another non-repetitive part to map on, and mapping's 108
  s could drop substantially for a small archive cost.

  No lever if work and entries fall together — e.g. cap=256 keeping 99% of
  entries and 95% of work. Then the 60-candidates-per-hit is spread across the
  whole index rather than concentrated in repeats, capping buys nothing you
  don't pay for in placements, and 279 s is the floor.

  The prior evidence points both ways, which is why it needed measuring: 60
  candidates per hit where uniform would give ~1 is a strong skew signal, but
  this project already measured frequency-ranked minimizers at +14% archive — a
  related idea that failed badly here.

  Gate is 3/3 byte-identical so far. The histogram runs last, after the four
  remaining gate datasets and the two HG002 timing runs — about 20 minutes.

● Checked all three against what the field would accept. There's one issue 
  underneath all of them: our outputs live in pseudogenome coordinates, every 
  competitor works in reference coordinates.

  T6a — arcs export vs SPAdes

  The weakest of the three. We aren't assembling; we're reading back a
  pseudogenome built at compress time. SPAdes builds one from scratch. So
  "50–200× faster" compares decompression to assembly.

  Worse, the pseudogenome is a compression artifact — a superstring of
  overlapping reads — not a biological assembly. There's no N50, genome
  fraction, or misassembly validation anywhere in this repo. A reviewer's first
  question is "is your exported FASTA a usable assembly?", and right now we
  can't answer.

  Two honest options: either state plainly that export is decompression and
  report the assembly cost that was paid at compression (~300 s on HG002, which
  we've now measured precisely), or run QUAST against the reference and earn the
  SPAdes comparison. Without one of those, drop the speedup claim.

  T6b — arcs coverage vs BWA+mosdepth

  Ours is per-contig coverage in pseudogenome space, free because placements are
  already stored. Theirs is per-base depth in reference space. Different
  granularity and different coordinates. The expected 2–5× is modest, and the
  defensible claim isn't speed — it's "coverage is a byproduct of the archive, 
  not a separate alignment." If biological interpretation is claimed, the
  contigs must be mapped to a reference, which re-incurs exactly the alignment
  we said we avoided.

  T6c — "no competitor exists" is factually wrong

  genocat --regions does regional extraction from compressed files, and samtools
  indexes CRAM for fast random access by region. Both are standard. A reviewer
  will know this immediately.

  The accurate statement is narrower: no competitor queries in pseudogenome 
  coordinates — because no competitor has a pseudogenome. That's a description
  of our data model, not a capability advantage. To make T6c meaningful you'd
  need reference-region → pseudogenome-coordinate translation, then compare
  against genocat --regions on the same biological region. That translation
  doesn't exist yet.

  Bottom line: T6b is defensible with reframing, T6a needs QUAST or a downgraded
  claim, and T6c's "unique" framing should go. None of this is new engineering
  — it's honesty about what each number compares.

  - Genozip: a universal extensible genomic data compressor

✻ Baked for 1m 47s · done Sunday 1:57 AM

❯ but will it genralize win?                                                    

● Honest answer: the direction should generalize, but a fixed 1024 should not 
  ship — and that's a real distinction.

  Why the direction generalizes: the cap is a threshold on a measured property
  (bucket size), not a behaviour change. On low-repeat genomes — E. coli, H.
  salinarum, most bacteria — the distribution is tight, almost nothing exceeds
  the cap, so it does nothing: no speedup, but also no size cost. On repeat-rich
  genomes — human, and the plant sets like U. gibba — the tail is fat, so it
  does a lot. It helps exactly where there is something to help, and is inert
  elsewhere. That's the good kind of generalization.

  Why a fixed 1024 is wrong anyway: this project has a standing rule that fixes
  must be formulas over a measured input property, never fitted constants. A
  bucket of 1024 in HG002's 15.3M-entry index is a very different thing from
  1024 in E. coli's ~2.5M-entry index. Shipping the literal number would be
  exactly the per-dataset tuning the rule forbids — and the rule exists because
  three fitted cost models were already discarded here.

  The generalizable form is to derive the cap from the distribution itself: the 
  smallest C retaining ≥X% of entries, computed in the same linear pass that
  already builds the histogram. That adapts automatically — small C on tight
  distributions where it costs nothing, ~1024 on human where the tail is fat —
  and it's keyed on measured data rather than on a constant I picked.

  So the sequence is: the running measurement establishes whether the trade is 
  worth anything at all (HG002 curve: caps 0/4096/1024/256/64) and whether it's 
  inert-or-positive on non-human data (5 datasets at cap=1024). If both hold, I
  convert the constant into the derived rule before it goes anywhere near a
  default — and re-gate.

  If the 5 non-human sets show a size cost without a speed gain, the cap is
  human-only and doesn't ship as a default at all.

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Done — the encoder now picks the cap itself, in one linear pass over the
  already-sorted index:

  ▎ take the smallest cap that still retains ≥99% of seed entries

  Self-scaling by construction: on a low-repeat genome the distribution is
  tight, so the rule lands on a small cap and discards essentially nothing; on a
  repeat-rich genome it lands exactly where the fat tail starts. On HG002 it
  will select 1024 (99.172% of entries, 20.3% of the work). Cost is two scans of
  a 122 MB array — ~0.05 s against a 108 s stage.

  This matters beyond convenience: a literal 1024 would have been a fitted
  constant, and a bucket of 1024 in HG002's 15.3M-entry index is a completely
  different object from 1024 in E. coli's ~2.5M-entry index. This project has
  already discarded three cost models for exactly that reason, so a hardcoded
  cap would have been the same mistake in new clothing.

  CAPS_SEEDCAP=N forces a cap, =0 disables it, CAPS_SEEDKEEP overrides the
  retained fraction — so the running curve measurement still works unchanged.

  Waiting on that curve now: HG002 at caps 0/4096/1024/256/64 (does the trade
  buy anything, and what does it cost in bytes), then cap=1024 on five non-human
  datasets (is it inert-or-positive where repeat structure is completely
  different). If the non-human arm shows size cost without speed gain, it
  doesn't ship as a default at all.

● Important — the guard I assumed is not the right one. The per-level filter is
  rlen[a] < L, which affects which reads are eligible at a level, not whether
  the two groups agree. Let me reason precisely rather than ship a wrong
  condition.

  Both groups start at L=Lmax and decrement identically. At any level L, tails
  is a function of (open_tails, L, rlen) — and open_tails only shrinks when
  nxt[a]!=NONE, i.e. from commits made at earlier (higher) levels. Since both
  groups run the identical loop from Lmax down to 51, every commit is identical 
  down to L=51 regardless of read-length variation — the divergence begins only
  when group B stops and group A continues to 16.

  So the sharing is valid for all datasets, not just fixed-length ones. My
  "min(rlen) ≥ max(MINOV)" guard was wrong, and shipping it would have
  needlessly disabled the optimization on variable-length data. Verifying that
  claim against the real logs before building on it:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

  ▎ Claim 3 is an amortization argument, not a speed contest. ARCS pays a 
  ▎ one-time cost of ~200 s to compress HG002 (4.28 GB), and that pass produces 
  ▎ a lossless archive and the pseudogenome as a byproduct. Once written, the 
  ▎ archive answers three questions at decompression speed: the assembled 
  ▎ sequence (6.0 s), per-contig coverage (7.8 s), and an arbitrary region (6.3 
  ▎ s). The comparison is not "our assembler beats SPAdes" — it is that a user 
  ▎ who compresses with SPRING must still run an assembler to obtain contigs, an
  ▎ aligner plus mosdepth to obtain depth, and cannot query a region at all 
  ▎ without decompressing the whole file. Against SPAdes the export margin is 
  ▎ large, but the fair comparator is MEGAHIT, which is ~6× faster than SPAdes; 
  ▎ the margin should be stated against both. The honest framing is: the 
  ▎ assembly cost is paid once, at compression time, and is already counted in 
  ▎ our T2 wall-clock — which is why ARCS is ~4× slower than SPRING to compress 
  ▎ and effectively free thereafter.

  T6a — export: reference-free assembly

  Use case: you don't have a reference, or can't trust one. Reference-based
  analysis "relies on public repositories having closely-related high quality 
  references, which is not guaranteed for arbitrary clinical isolates." And
  surveillance today "requires a priori knowledge of the pathogen of interest… 
  cannot detect the emergence of completely novel pathogens."

  Concrete: hospital outbreak investigation — de novo assemble each isolate,
  cluster, count SNP distances, identify transmission chains. Novel-pathogen
  detection. Metagenomics, where most organisms have no reference at all.

  Our pitch: you archived the reads anyway; the contigs are already inside the
  archive.

  Use case: is this sequencing run usable, and are there dosage changes?
  Coverage is used "to assess the quality of sequencing data (such as 
  calculating the percentage of genome with ≥30× read depth) or to identify 
  genomic regions with insufficient reads for reliable variant calling", and
  it's the input to copy-number variant detection.

  uniformity and relative depth, not "coverage at chr20:31,000,000." For the QC
  application that's often enough; for CNV at a locus it isn't, without a
  coordinate mapping we don't have.

  T6c — query: retrieval without full decompression

  Use case: pull a subset from cold storage. Archives are terabytes; you want
  the reads over one locus without inflating the whole file — re-analysis of one
  gene, checking a variant, sharing a slice.

  Honest limit: this is the weakest of the three. genocat --regions and indexed

  capability demonstration, not a competitive win.

● Web Search("genozip genocat FASTQ compression reference-free reference-based
            algorithm how it works")
  ⎿  Did 1 search in 7s

● One line: Genozip/genocat supports both — reference-free by default, and 
  reference-based as an optional add-on that improves ratio.

  How, specifically: when you don't give it a reference, Genozip compresses
  FASTQ with its own general-purpose codecs (context modeling per field —
  sequence, quality, IDs — no assembly, no pseudogenome). When you do supply a
  reference, it aligns each read against it and stores the alignment (edit ops)
  instead of the raw bases — that's the reference-based path, and it's what
  boosts its ratio.

  genocat's --regions, though, is a different thing again — and this is the part
  that matters for our T6c comparison. --regions extracts by reference 
  coordinate, which only works when the file was compressed with a reference (or
  is SAM/BAM/CRAM, which always carries reference coordinates by construction).
  On a reference-free FASTQ compress, genocat has record IDs and file order,
  but no genomic coordinate to filter on — so --regions isn't applicable there
  at all.

  That's an important correction to what I told you earlier: it's not simply
  "genocat does the same thing we do." A fair T6c benchmark needs Genozip run in
  reference-based mode (supply chr20, same reference we'd use for coordinate
  context) before genocat --regions is even a valid comparator.
  Reference-free-vs-reference-free, genocat has nothing to query by coordinate
  at all — which is actually a point in our favor, since our query works with no
  reference supplied.

  Sources: Genozip: a universal extensible genomic data compressor · Command: 
  genocat · Deep FASTQ and BAM co-compression in Genozip 15

✻ Crunched for 25s · done Sunday 3:04 AM

❯ genocat's --regions,  so this again not apples to apples rught                

● Right — not apples to apples, and I should say plainly which direction it
  cuts.

  The mismatch: genocat --regions needs a reference genome coordinate system to
  filter on — it only works if the archive was compressed with a reference
  supplied (or is SAM/BAM/CRAM, which always carries one). Our arcs query takes
  a pseudogenome offset, built from the reads alone, no reference at all.

  So there's no configuration where both tools answer the same question on equal
  footing:

  - Genozip reference-free (fair compression comparison) → --regions has no
    genomic coordinate to filter on. Not usable at all.
  - Genozip reference-based (supply chr20) → --regions becomes usable, but now
    Genozip gets to exploit a reference we didn't give ourselves. Any speed or
    size difference partly reflects "one tool got a reference and one didn't,"
    not engineering.

  That's exactly the same shape of problem as SPAdes/MEGAHIT in T6a — different
  inputs to reach a comparable output. There, the fix was to state it plainly
  (assembly cost paid once, at compression time) rather than force a bar-chart
  comparison. The honest fix here is the same: state that no reference-free tool
  offers coordinate-range query at all, and if a reference-based number against
  Genozip is reported, label it explicitly as reference-based-vs-reference-free
  — not a same-category speed race.

  That also means my earlier claim needs one more correction: it's not "genocat
  --regions exists so our uniqueness claim is false." It's narrower and still
  true in the way that matters — no reference-free tool does coordinate query,
  which is the actual claim T6c should make.

● B is now actually built, not just described — here's the full accounting.

  What it does: the two MINOV groups' round-2 sweeps are identical down to the
  shallower group's floor (proven from production logs: ERR5181310's two groups
  show a strict probes/links superset — 10,295→14,543, 18→21 — exactly the "same
  prefix, one continues" signature). So the sweep now runs to that shared depth
  once, in the parent, before any fork; the shallow group inherits the finished
  state via copy-on-write and does zero additional sweeping, and the deep group
  continues the identical loop from that point instead of restarting at Lmax.

  Why this was riskier than A, and why I built it carefully rather than fast:
  sweep() unconditionally resets nxt/prv/ovl/ch_h/ch_t and rebuilds open_tails
  at the top of every call — I checked this before touching anything, because if
  I'd missed it, "continue from L=50" would have silently wiped the very state
  it needed to continue from. The fix is a cont/startL pair on the lambda that
  skips the reset only when explicitly asked, defaulting to today's exact
  behavior everywhere else (round 1, second-region sweep, all untouched).

  Gate running now, 8 datasets — deliberately including ERR5181310 (SARS-CoV-2,
  19 distinct read lengths, 40–221 bp), the case most likely to break if my
  open_tails reasoning were wrong, plus a CAPS_CALL check to confirm Claim 2's
  path is unaffected.

  I will not report a timing number until this comes back byte-identical —
  that's the same rule that caught mext and the quality-strategy cut earlier
  today.

● Lever B: 8/8 BYTE-IDENTICAL, including SARS-CoV-2 (variable-length, highest
  risk). CAPS_CALL check finishing now.

  Now the deep answer to the goal, worked from first principles rather than
  guessed.

  Why there's no free version of C

  MAXMAP (which the two-level fork already shares across candidates) and MINOV
  are fundamentally different kinds of parameters:

  - MAXMAP is a pure acceptance threshold applied after the mapping search — the
    search itself doesn't depend on it, which is exactly why sharing it worked
    (proven: cumulative histogram sums reproduced every candidate's mapped=
    count exactly).
  - MINOV is a search-depth parameter that changes which reads chain at all. A
    lower MINOV finds a strict superset of chains (confirmed again just now:
    SRR40271341's links go 118,995→127,373 as MINOV drops). That means the two
    MINOV values produce two genuinely different pseudogenomes — not the same
    computation viewed through different thresholds. Mapping and MEM run on that
    pg, so they cannot be shared; they're not redundant computation, they're
    computation on different inputs.

  So the real question for C is narrower: can we predict, cheaply, which pg will
  compress smaller — without running MEM on both?

  I checked this from two directions:

  1. Empirically, already tested and it fails: pg after chains doesn't predict
     the winner. HG002 picks the larger pg (160.4 MB); ERR552797 picks the
     smaller. Inconsistent sign, no threshold works.
  2. From first principles, and this is the part that explains why it fails: the
     archive size is dominated by what MEM's self-match removes from the main
     pg (69.4% on HG002), and that self-match ratio depends on the pg's internal
     repeat structure, not its size. A larger pg with more redundant repeat
     content can compress smaller after MEM than a tighter pg with less to
     remove. There is no O(1) proxy for "how much internal redundancy does this
     pg have" — that's what MEM's linear scan measures, not something knowable
     before running it.

  Building a fitted threshold on top of that (e.g. weighting pg size + leftover
  count) would be inventing cost model #4, and this project's own memory
  (reimpl_algorithmic_first_principle, three discarded models at 45–55% error)
  says exactly why that fails: it's not that nobody found the right
  coefficients, it's that the quantity being predicted isn't linearly related to
  what's cheap to measure.

  The honest reduction that's real

  Lever B already ate into C's savings without touching MINOV grouping at all.
  Before B, "2 groups" meant recomputing the round-2 sweep from Lmax twice —
  that duplication is gone. What C would still save, on top of B, is only the
  divergent tail: mapping + MEM + coding for the second group. Waiting for B's

● Summary of the "achieve C's speedup without losing size" question, structural 
  not speculative:

  No free version exists, and I can now say precisely why. MAXMAP and MINOV are
  different in kind — MAXMAP is an acceptance threshold applied after a shared
  search (which is why sharing it worked, proven by exact histogram
  reconstruction). MINOV changes which reads chain at all, so it produces two 
  genuinely different pseudogenomes, not two views of one computation. What
  decides the winner is how much internal repeat redundancy each pg has, which
  is exactly what MEM's linear scan measures — there's no cheaper proxy for it,
  confirmed both empirically (pg after chains picks the wrong sign on HG002 vs
  ERR552797) and structurally (the quantity isn't linearly related to anything
  cheap to compute before running MEM).

  Building a predictor anyway would be this project's fourth fitted cost model;
  the first three are on record at 45–55% error and were discarded per the
  standing rule. I'm not going to repeat that under time pressure just to appear
  to have solved it.

  What I did find, and built instead: lever B already captures the part of C's 
  saving that was free. Before B, "2 groups" duplicated the round-2 sweep from
  Lmax twice; that duplication is now gone, gated 8/8 byte-identical including 
  the variable-length case, with the CAPS_CALL path confirmed unaffected. What C
  would still remove on top of B is only the genuinely divergent tail — mapping
  + MEM + coding for the second group — and that residual is what the running
  HG002 timing will report exactly, so the size-for-speed decision on C is made
  with real numbers instead of the original rough estimate.

● Tested it against the full panel rather than a couple of datasets — and it's a
  genuine no, with the receipts.

  leftover_frac (round 2's leftover count — a free signal, available before
  mapping or MEM ever run) is the natural candidate: "pick whichever MINOV
  chained more reads." Checked against all 13 known winners:

  CORRECT (low leftover_frac = winner):  ERR552797, SRR2584863, SRR32429602,
                                          SRR36741279, SRR37283774, SRR39257532,
  SRR554369   (7)
  WRONG:                                 DRR976266, ERR12954017, ERR17740259,
                                          ERR5181310, HG002, SRR40271341
               (6)

  7/13 correct — 53.8%, statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip. And
  it's wrong on exactly the dataset that matters most: HG002 has leftover_frac
  0.168 (MINOV=16) vs 0.174 (MINOV=51), so "pick lower" says 16 — but the real
  winner is 51.

  This isn't a small-sample fluke, it's the structural point I made earlier
  landing concretely: the archive-size winner is decided by MEM's self-match 
  ratio, and that ratio depends on the pg's internal repeat structure, not on 
  how many reads got chained. A dataset can have more leftovers and still win,
  because its main pg happens to be more redundant and MEM crunches it harder.
  Nothing computed before MEM runs carries that information.

  So the direct answer: no — not "much less than 0.629%." A cheap adaptive
  picker doesn't help, because a coin-flip predictor doesn't reduce worst-case
  cost at all (worst case is set by the single largest individual miss, and a
  50/50 rule still hits misses). The only ways to actually beat 0.629% are
  either (a) run both mapping+MEM cheaply enough that duplicating them stops
  mattering — which is what B already did for the sweep, and mapping/MEM are the
  next targets I haven't found a lever for — or (b) accept the 0.629% and take
  C outright, which stays your call.

● Lever B is a measured regression, not a win — reporting immediately, no spin.

  cap_va  (no lever B):        197.83 s
  cap_vB  (with lever B):      230.15 s / 234.69 s     ← 16–19% SLOWER
                                round2 stage: 13.00/17.78 s  (genuinely tiny
  now)
                                archive: byte-identical throughout

  Round 2 itself got dramatically cheaper — 13–18 s versus ~55–66 s before — 
  exactly as designed. But the total got worse. Here's why, and it's a real
  structural lesson, not a bug:

  Before lever B, the two groups forked immediately after round 1 and each ran
  its own full sweep concurrently, at 6 threads apiece. The "duplicated" shared
  prefix cost nothing extra in wall-clock time, because both copies were
  computed in parallel by two independent processes — the wall-clock cost was
  max(group1, group2), not the sum.

  After lever B, I moved that shared prefix into the parent, serially, before 
  the fork — turning two-processes-running-concurrently into
  one-stage-then-fork. That's genuinely less total CPU work, but the sweep is
  ~31% serial (commit phase, from the earlier CAPS_SWEEP_TIMING data) — an
  Amdahl ceiling that doesn't shrink with more threads. Removing the redundancy
  this way converted hidden, free concurrency into a new sequential stage, and
  the serial-commit cost of that stage no longer benefits from a second process
  also making progress at the same time.

  Reverting now, with the reasoning recorded so this exact mistake — "less total
  work" ≠ "less wall time" when the removed redundancy was previously hidden by
  concurrency — doesn't get repeated.

● Genuine assessment, not spin:

  On its own, the Claim 1 speed number is a real, disclosed weakness — say so 
  plainly, don't dress it up. We're still ~4× slower than SPRING (198 s vs ~53
  s) after clawing back from 17×. A reviewer looking at T2 alone will note that.

  But that's the wrong comparison to lead with, and here's the researcher's 
  reasoning for why. SPRING is a streaming compressor with no assembly step — it
  can't give you a genome, SNV calls, or coverage. Our actual competitor class
  is PgRC2 (assembly-based, same architecture), and PgRC2's own paper states
  plainly that assembly-based compressors trade time for ratio against streaming
  tools — that's an accepted, well-established point in this literature's
  tradeoff space, not a novel failure mode we're introducing. Our real edge
  there is +1.88% smaller than PgRC2, which is real but modest, not a blowout
  (PgRC2 itself claims up to 18–21% over SPRING/Minicom). I don't have PgRC2's
  speed in front of me from today's numbers, and that's the comparison that
  actually matters for this axis — I'd flag that as a gap to close before
  publication, not assume it favorably.

  The "other perks" you're pointing at are the actual thesis, not an accessory.
  The honest framing isn't "we compress 4% smaller and 4× slower" — it's "one
  198 s pass gives you the archive and the assembly and SNV calls and coverage,
  where the conventional alternative is SPRING (53 s) + SPAdes (258 s) +
  DiscoSNP++ (76.5 s) + BWA/mosdepth, which is already more wall-clock than we
  spend total, before counting three separate tools and three separate outputs
  to manage." That's a legitimate systems-paper structure — pay once at
  compression time, amortize across three claims — and it's the frame under
  which the 4× speed cost reads as the price of assembly, not as inefficiency.

  Why I believe that price is close to the honest floor, not a sign we 
  under-optimized: every attempted free win today failed for a principled reason
  I could name afterward — MEM is bandwidth-bound so fewer candidates didn't
  help; the sweep-prefix duplication was already hidden by free concurrency, so
  serializing it made things worse. That's evidence the remaining cost is the
  actual work the method requires, not slack.

  What I'd tell a co-author before submission: ship the 4.6× improvement and the
  honest 4× gap to SPRING with the amortization framing front and center, get
  the PgRC2 speed number before claiming parity with our real competitor class,
  and don't let T2 stand alone in the paper without the multi-claim total next
  to it — that's the number that actually makes the case.

● Yes — that's exactly right, and it's worth being precise about why, because
  that precision is what makes it a real contribution rather than three separate
  demos.

  The single insight: a pseudogenome is not a compression artifact you throw 
  away — it's a data structure you keep. Once you've built it, you've already
  paid for three things other tools pay for separately:

  1. An assembly (Claim 1's byproduct → Claim 3's export). SPAdes/MEGAHIT do de
     Bruijn graph construction from scratch every time you want contigs. We
     already built an equivalent structure to compress the reads in the first
     place — exporting it is a stream decode, not a computation.
  2. Read placements (→ Claim 3's coverage). Every read's position in the
     pseudogenome is stored to make decompression possible. Coverage is a
     difference-array over positions you already have — no alignment step,
     because there was nothing to align to (no reference), just positions you
     already recorded.
  3. A k-mer graph over real, assembled sequence (→ Claim 2's calling).
     DiscoSNP++ builds a de Bruijn graph from raw reads and walks it for
     bubbles. Method B reuses the encoder's own contigs and skips
     build_substrate — the read-placement step DiscoSNP++ pays 738 s for on
     chr20, because our contigs already exist.

  So the honest one-line thesis is: compression forces you to solve "how do
  these reads fit together" once, and that solved structure is reusable as an
  assembly, a coverage map, and a variant-calling substrate — for free, because
  none of those are separate computations, they're different views of the same
  object.

  Why this is the load-bearing claim, and why today's speed work had to respect 
  it: every gate today checked byte-identity for exactly this reason — if a
  speed change had altered the pseudogenome even slightly, it wouldn't just cost
  Claim 1 size, it would silently corrupt Claim 2's F1 and Claim 3's exported
  assembly too, since they all read the same structure. That's not incidental
  caution; it's the direct consequence of the architecture being genuinely
  unified rather than three tools sharing a repo.

  Where I'd be careful not to oversell it: the quality of what falls out isn't
  automatically as good as a purpose-built tool would produce standalone — Claim
  2 is het-SNV only (indels are structurally capped), and Claim 3's query works
  in pseudogenome coordinates, not reference coordinates, so it needs
  translation to be biologically actionable in the way a genomicist expects. The
  insight buys you the capability and the speed; it doesn't buy you parity with
  a specialist tool on every axis. That's a fair trade to state plainly, not a
  flaw to hide.

● Here's what I've established about their engineering while that finishes —
  this is the part nobody had documented:

  What DiscoSNP++/GATB actually does

  1. Bounded memory is their default, not their fallback.
  estimated_kmers_volume: 11,304 MB     ← what the k-mers would cost raw
  max_memory: 5000                      ← what they allow themselves
  nb_partitions: 24                     ← so they partition, always
  nb_partitions_in_parallel: 12         ← 12 at once, 1 core each
  mini_size: 10, kmc2 heuristic         ← minimizer-grouped for locality
  They never consider holding it all in RAM. We built the same machinery
  (superkmer spill, minimizer-grouped, 2-bit packed) and measured it at 25.4 s /
  ~7 GB vs 191.7 s / 28.3 GB in-RAM — ours is also better when it runs — but
  our ceiling is 60% of free RAM, so a roomy box silently takes the bad path.
  Their budget is declared; ours is opportunistic. That's the single 
  transferable lesson.

  2. They process fewer k-mers by design.
  1,481,732,372 raw  →  57.2% discarded as weak  →  60,292,781 solid
  ours: 140,719,632 kept  (2.33× more)
  abundance_min: 3 vs our MINC=2. This is not them being cleverer — it's the
  same knob that costs them recall. Our docs are explicit that the 2–4 count
  band is "where low-coverage het alleles live," and that's why we're 0.879 vs
  their 0.847 on SNV F1. We're buying recall with k-mers.

  3. Their time is spent differently:
  graph creation 23 s | bubble detection 32 s | VCF 8 s = 76 s
  ours: kc_H_build 191.7 s (in-RAM) or ~25 s (spill) | coherence 24.9 s |
  traversal 62.2 s
  Their graph creation (23 s) is comparable to our spill-path counting (~25 s).
  Their bubble detection (32 s) beats our traversal+coherence (~87 s) — but
  they're walking 60.3M nodes to our 140.7M, so roughly 2.3× less graph.
  Normalized, the gap largely closes.

  The honest conclusion so far: they aren't out-engineering us on the k-mer
  counter — our spill path matches their graph-creation time. They're ahead
  because (a) they always run the bounded path, and (b) they carry half the
  graph, which is the same choice that makes them less sensitive than us. The
  one thing to genuinely take is the declared-budget default.

  The honest answer on halving:

  Time — no free path. We're at parity or better on every stage per unit of 
  work. The entire 1.39× gap is that we carry 140.7M k-mers to their 60.3M,
  because abundance_min=3 discards the 2–4 count band. That band is where our
  recall advantage lives (SNV F1 0.879 vs 0.847). Halving time means adopting
  their threshold and handing back the accuracy win — that's a product decision,
  not an optimization.

  RAM — bounded by what the caller genuinely needs. The 3,205 MB still resident
  at caller entry is packed reads, quality, contigs, per-read placements, and
  the pseudogenome — all things the caller actually reads. Below that requires
  not co-residing with compression, i.e. a separate calling pass over a stored
  archive. That machinery exists (capsule_decode call) but I tested it today and
  it's genuinely broken — it carries 0 read placements, reconstructs 2 contigs
  instead of thousands, and calls diploid where the real path calls haploid.
  Fixing it properly is real engineering with F1 risk, not a quick win.

  So: both remaining halvings cost something real — one costs recall, the other
  needs an architecture change. Everything that was free, I've now taken.

❯ but i dont get we are lighter and all but y not faster                        

● Because efficiency and workload are two different things, and ours is the
  bigger number:

                          ours          theirs        ratio
  k-mers carried        140.7 M         60.3 M       2.33× MORE work
  speed per node        437 ns/1k      531 ns/1k     1.21× FASTER
                                                     ─────────────
  bubble phase          61.6 s          32 s         2.33 ÷ 1.21 = 1.93× slower
                                                     (observed: 1.92×)

  We're 1.21× more efficient but doing 2.33× more work. Efficiency loses that 
  fight. Being better per node doesn't rescue you when you're walking more than
  twice as many nodes.

  Same story on RAM, except there the efficiency gap is large enough to win:

                          ours          theirs
  k-mers held           140.7 M         60.3 M
  caller RAM            2.97 GB        3.29 GB
  bytes per k-mer         21.1           54.5      ← we're 2.6× more
  space-efficient

  2.6× efficiency beats 2.33× workload → we come out lighter. On time, 1.21×
  efficiency loses to 2.33× workload → we come out slower. Same two numbers,
  different outcome, purely because our memory engineering is proportionally
  further ahead than our traversal engineering.

  And the 2.33× isn't waste — it's the product. They set abundance_min=3 and
  drop every k-mer seen once or twice. We set MINC=2 and keep the 2-count band,
  because that's where low-coverage heterozygous alleles live. That extra 80.4M
  k-mers is what makes our SNV F1 0.879 against their 0.847.

  So the honest framing: we're not slower because we're worse-built, we're 
  slower because we're looking harder. To match their 75 s we'd adopt
  abundance_min=3 and hand back the recall lead — the number the claim rests on.

  The one place there's genuine, unexploited slack is emission: ~19 s for us vs
  8 s for them, and that's not explained by node count. That's the only stage
  where we're actually behind on engineering rather than on workload.

● Web Search("pileup variant calling from de novo assembly contigs reads aligned
            back accuracy vs de Bruijn bubble calling")
  ⎿  Did 1 search in 8s

● This is the answer to your question, and the literature is blunt about it.

  From the comparison studies:

  ▎ the de Bruijn graph error correction process can collapse reads from two 
  ▎ alleles into a single haplotype, resulting in homozygous SNVs being called 
  ▎ correctly whereas heterozygous SNVs would have no more than 50% chance to be
  ▎ called correctly

  ▎ Assembly-based approaches had a much lower recall rate and precision 
  ▎ compared to alignment-based approaches, which recovered 99% of imputed SNVs

  ▎ there is a positional bias in variant calling against draft assemblies built
  ▎ from de Bruijn graphs, with unexpectedly high numbers of variants at 
  ▎ positions related to k-mer or read length

  Claim 2 is a het-SNV claim. The dBG bubble method is documented as the weakest
  available approach for exactly that.

  And here's why we're doing it anyway: we copied it from someone who had no 
  choice. DiscoSNP++ has only raw reads — no reference, no alignment — so
  bubbles are the only thing available to them. Every alternative I found (SKA
  lo, LueVari, EBWT2INDEL, the distributed pipeline) is stuck in that same
  paradigm for the same reason.

  We are not in that position. Our own log says it:

  [PLACE] carried 12604917 read placements from the encoder

  Compression already told us which read sits at which position in which contig,
  with orientation and clipping. That is what alignment produces — the input
  the literature says gives the better method. We get it as a byproduct, and
  then throw it away to go build a 140.7M-node k-mer graph and hunt bubbles
  instead.

  That graph is ~85 s of our 105 s and the bulk of the caller's RAM:

  kc_H_build    23.2 s  + ~2.4 GB   ← counting k-mers we already have placements
  for
  traversal     61.6 s              ← walking a graph to rediscover adjacency we
  know
  ─────────────────────────
                84.8 s of 105.1 s

  So the honest answer to "why do the same thing they did, twice over": we 
  shouldn't. Not for speed reasons — for accuracy reasons that happen to also be
  speed reasons. The pileup path exists in our code already (build_substrate +
  the parallel pileup, which is what the full CAPS_CALL path runs), and our own
  window numbers put it at F1 0.888/0.877 versus the published dBG number of
  0.879.

  The genuinely interesting experiment is therefore not "make the graph faster"
  but "does the placement-based pileup beat the bubble caller on full chr20, 
  without building the graph at all?" — which would be simultaneously more
  accurate per the literature, ~85 s cheaper, and several GB lighter. That's the
  paradigm question, and it's testable with code that already exists.

  Sources: alignment vs assembly-based SNV calling · positional bias in dBG 
  draft assemblies · SKA lo · EBWT2INDEL · LueVari

  - alignment-based = align reads to a reference genome

  taxonomy B is assembly-based too. So are A and B both. I took a finding about
  reference alignment and mapped it onto a reference-free pileup, which is a
  category error: the thing that makes their alignment-based approach recover
  99% is precisely the reference, which a reference-free tool by definition does
  not have.

● Short answer: the literature says assembly-based is weak relative to reference
  alignment — and reference alignment is exactly the thing we're not allowed to
  have.

  Xu et al. rank two options:

  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │                 │      uses a reference?       │     their verdict      │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ alignment-based │ yes — reads aligned to the   │ recovers 99% of SNVs   │
  │                 │ reference genome             │                        │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ assembly-based  │ no — assemble, then call     │ "much lower recall and │
  │                 │                              │  precision"            │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘

  So it's not a statement that assembly is bad in the abstract. It's a statement
  that not having a reference costs you accuracy. That's a real and
  unsurprising finding.

  Which makes it useless for our decision, in two ways:

  1. We can't take the winning side. Reference-free calling is Claim 2. The 99%
     arm requires GRCh37 — the moment you use it, you're not doing what we claim
     to do. It's not an option we declined; it's an option the claim forbids.
  2. Both of our candidates are on the losing side. A (bubbles) and B (pileup on
     our own pseudogenome) are both assembly-based in their taxonomy. The paper
     ranks assembly vs reference — it never ranks two assembly-based methods
     against each other. So it had zero predictive content about whether A or B
     would win. I read a ranking that wasn't in the paper.

  That's why the measurement was the only way to settle it, and why B losing
  isn't a surprise the literature should have prevented.

  The practical consequence is what matters for the paper: our comparison class
  is other reference-free tools, and there we're ahead — DiscoSNP++ 0.847 vs our
  0.8766 on the same box, same input, same scoring. The Xu et al. gap to
  reference alignment is a limitation we disclose (a reference-free method is
  expected to trail a reference-based one), not a benchmark we're failing to
  meet.

  And it doesn't touch the finding that actually drives the work now: the
  graph's 7,720 misses are 3× enriched for variants within one k-mer. That came
  from our own data, not from anyone's paper.

● Short answers:

  1. Does pileup work? Yes — it works, it just loses. P=0.963 (better than
  bubbles' 0.933), R=0.695 (much worse than 0.827). Valid calls, too few of
  them.

  2. Did we do it wrong? Partly — and I can't cleanly separate the two. That
  precision/recall pattern is the signature of correct machinery on a lossy
  substrate, not broken machinery. The trail: 116,249 candidates → 43,708 SNVs →
  36,041 survive the lift. The losses are in the collapse step, not the pileup
  math. The code itself says collapse is required (it's what puts both alleles
  in one frame) but collapse also merges contigs that shouldn't merge, and each
  merge deletes sites. So the honest verdict is "pileup over our collapsed 
  substrate loses recall," not "pileup is a worse method." Those are different
  claims and only the first is supported.

  3. What literature says about pileup: it's the standard method — samtools
  mpileup, GATK, VarScan all do it — but always against a reference. There is no
  established literature on pileup over a self-assembled reference-free
  pseudogenome, because nobody does that. So literature neither validates nor
  refutes our B. That's also why my earlier citation was wrong: I borrowed the
  reputation of reference-pileup for something that isn't reference-pileup.

  What this means practically: B is not proof the paradigm is dead. It's proof
  this substrate caps recall at 0.695. If collapse were the only problem, a
  better substrate could beat A. But that's a hypothesis, and it costs 852 s and
  14 GB to test again — versus the encoder channels which cost ~0 and are
  already running.

  So I'm not chasing the substrate. The measured facts that matter: bubbles win
  at 106 s, and the 7,720 sites they miss are 3× enriched for clustered variants
  — which is where the free channels get their shot.

  - if it grows the archive → calling is taxing compression, and the fusion

  One flaw in E's design I want on record before its numbers arrive, so I don't

  pseudogenome carries both haplotypes plus repeats, so multiple contigs

● Short answer: timing isn't the issue — A already runs during compression. The

  Two different ideas, and it's worth separating them:

  Idea 1 — run DiscoSNP during compression, store the resulting calls in the 
  archive.
  We effectively already do the first half: CAPS_CALL=1 runs the caller inside
  the compressor process, in the same pass. Storing the output VCF in the
  archive too would just be caching a result. It doesn't make compression
  better, it doesn't make calling better, and anyone can do it. Not novel.

  Idea 2 — the archive already contains the raw material for calling, so read 
  the calls out of it.
  This is D and E, and yes, this is what I mean.

  The distinction that matters: in E, those 2.53 MB of mismatch records are not 
  stored for calling. They're stored because decode is impossible without them —
  they're how the compressor remembers that read X differed from region Y at
  position Z. A compressor is forced to record every difference between two
  copies of the same locus, and that set of differences is exactly what a
  het-SNV caller is looking for.

  So:

  ┌────────┬────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │        │       what's in the archive        │    who could claim it    │
  ├────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ Idea 1 │ a VCF someone computed             │ anyone — it's a cache    │
  ├────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ Idea 2 │ mismatch records required for      │ only a tool that both    │
  │  (E)   │ losslessness, read as variants     │ compresses and calls     │
  └────────┴────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

  A's real defect is not that it runs at the wrong time. It's that it ignores 
  the archive and rebuilds everything from the reads with a k-mer graph — so the
  fact that it runs inside compression buys convenience and nothing else.

  That's the whole reason I'm measuring E: it's the only version where the
  answer to "what does compression contribute?" is something other than
  "nothing."

  Let me state the bar the sweep has to clear, before I see the numbers, so I

  improves F1 only if:

  F1' = (73710 + 2ΔTP) / (84085 + ΔTP + ΔFP)  >  0.8766

    →  marginal precision of the added calls must exceed ~44%

  positives — 0.5%, catastrophically short. The question is whether RC≥3 or the
  MMCNT=1 subset concentrates the signal by the required two orders of
  magnitude.

  high-recall, low-precision candidate generator — genuinely finding 72% of what
  the graph misses, but not separable enough to use as a caller on its own
  evidence. That would still be a real finding, and it would point at the
  obvious next lever: the base qualities, which the caller uses at QMIN=20 and
  these encoder channels currently ignore entirely.

  Indexing insight that makes this cheap: reads are 2-bit packed with woff[u]

  Two facts that matter: E's raw recall (0.9009) is higher than the published 
  caller's (0.8268), and it finds 72% of the sites the graph cannot. Both are
  real. But it can't be filtered into calls — best union F1 0.8739 vs A's
  0.8766.

  Novelty vs prior art

  As a source of variant candidates, E has no precedent I could find. Every
  reference-free caller builds an index or graph from raw reads and hunts
  bubbles:

  ┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
  │         tool         │             approach              │    needs     │
  │                      │                                   │  reference?  │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ DiscoSNP++, kSNP,    │ k-mer / dBG bubbles from raw      │ no           │
  │ SKA lo, Kmer2SNP     │ reads                             │              │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ EBWT2INDEL, LueVari  │ BWT / read-coloured dBG from raw  │ no           │
  │                      │ reads                             │              │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ ROVER                │ read-pair overlap,                │ yes          │
  │                      │ alignment-based                   │              │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ CALQ                 │ uses alignment to tune quality    │ yes          │
  │                      │ quantization, calls separately    │              │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ PgRC2, SPRING        │ compress only — no caller at all  │ —            │
  └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┘

  E is different in kind: the candidates are a re-reading of bytes the 
  compressor wrote to record how one region differs from another. No index is
  built, no graph traversed, no pass over the reads. Nothing in the literature
  derives calls from a compressor's back-reference mismatch stream, because no
  compressor ships with a caller to want them.

  So the novelty is genuine but it is a characterization, not a method. The
  honest one-line version:

  ▎ A pseudogenome compressor's back-reference mismatch records already contain 
  ▎ 90% of a sample's heterozygous SNVs, including 72% of those a de Bruijn 
  ▎ bubble caller structurally cannot reach — at ~1 byte per candidate.

  That sentence is new, true, and measured. What does not follow is "therefore
  compression replaces a caller," because the same measurement shows the records
  lack the evidence to separate the 40,159 true sites from 1.09 M errors.

  Why it fails, precisely

  Its evidence describes the anchor, not the allele. MLEN/MMCNT/RC say how long
  and clean the matched region was — which selects for unique, well-covered
  sequence, exactly where the graph already succeeds. At the best precision
  setting, 9,142 TPs contained only 676 rescues; the other 8,466 duplicated A.
  And recurrence is actively anti-correlated with truth (2.96% base rate → 1.4%
  at RC≥5), because in a pseudogenome stitching both haplotypes and repeats,
  "many regions disagree here" means repeat.

  Contrast with D (near-miss), where I added a true allele fraction: precision
  0.416 → 0.754, marginal precision 7.5% → 25.0%. Allele evidence works; anchor 
  evidence doesn't. E has no allele evidence available even in principle,
  because the two haplotypes are stitched into different places — there is no
  locus at which to count them.

  Verdict: E is a publishable observation in Discussion, not a claimable method.
  Claiming it as a caller would not survive a reviewer running the precision
  number.

● Because E alone is a far worse caller. Here are the numbers side by side:

  ┌───────────┬───────────────────┬───────────────┐
  │           │ E (best possible) │ A (published) │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ F1        │ 0.4909            │ 0.8766        │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ precision │ 0.434             │ 0.933         │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ recall    │ 0.565             │ 0.827         │
  └───────────┴───────────────────┴───────────────┘

  I swept ten filters on E. Its best F1 was 0.49 — barely half of A. So E cannot
  replace A.

  Why, in one sentence

  E finds more true variants than A, but buries them in a million false ones, 
  and there is no way to tell them apart.

  E unfiltered:  40,159 true   +  1,087,454 false     (recall 0.90, precision
  0.036)
  A:             36,855 true   +      2,655 false     (recall 0.83, precision
  0.93)

  E genuinely sees more of the real variants (90% vs 83%). But for every true
  one it emits ~27 false ones. Filtering hard enough to clean that up throws
  away the true ones too — at precision 0.779 it retains only 1,173 of the
  40,159.

  The root cause — and it's structural, not fixable by tuning

  E's only evidence describes the anchor: how long the matched region was
  (MLEN), how many mismatches it had (MMCNT), how many regions agree (RC). None
  of that says anything about the allele.

  A real caller asks one question: "is the support ~50/50 at this locus?" —
  that's what heterozygous means. E cannot ask it, because the pseudogenome 
  contains no pileup. Compression stitches the two haplotypes into different 
  places in the file, so there is no single locus where you could count REF vs
  ALT reads.

  That's why every anchor filter made it worse in a specific way: long clean
  anchors sit in unique, well-covered sequence — exactly where A already
  succeeds. At E's best precision setting, 9,142 of its true positives were
  sites A already found; only 676 were new.

  What E is actually good for

  Not as a caller — as a finding:

  ▎ The compressor's mismatch records already contain 90% of the sample's 
  ▎ het-SNVs, including 72% of the ones the k-mer graph structurally cannot 
  ▎ reach, at ~1 byte each.

  True, measured, and nobody has reported it. It goes in the Discussion. A ships
  as Claim 2.

  REF = reads placed at p that agree      (nmcov — already computed)
  ALT = distinct references disagreeing at p
  VAF = ALT / (ALT + REF)

  So my statement that "E has no allele evidence available even in principle"
  was too strong. It has no per-read pileup, but it does have the same
  agree/disagree denominator that worked for D.

  This is worth doing before we settle the story, because if VAF lifts E the way
  it lifted D, the high-novelty channel gets its fair shot — and that's the one
  that answers "this isn't just SPRING plus DiscoSNP."

  and the mismatch records give how many disagree there. That's the same

● Refuted immediately, and it puts my earlier statement back:

  [MM-VAF] denominator built over 93,237,625 bp from 612,053 refs
  VAF 1.0 : 932,236     ← essentially every record
  VAF 0.0 : 754

  COV=1 everywhere. The reason is structural: MEM references tile the
  pseudogenome — each destination position is encoded exactly once, either as
  literal or as one back-reference. 612,053 refs covering 93 Mbp is ~1.0× by
  construction. There is no second reference to disagree with, so ALT/COV is
  always 1/1.

  So I have to correct my correction. I said my original claim — "E has no
  allele evidence available even in principle" — was too strong. I built the fix
  to prove it. The data says the original claim was right, and for a sharper
  reason than I first gave:

  - the pseudogenome has no read pileup (haplotypes stitched to different
    places)
  - MEM references have no region pileup either (they tile, coverage ≡ 1)

  mem_extmm records are region-level disagreements — "this region differs from
  that region here." A variant allele fraction needs read-level counts at one
  locus, and that quantity does not exist anywhere in E's data, at either level.
  This is not a missing feature; it's what the encoding is.

  That's why D could be fixed and E cannot: near-miss records individual 
  rejected reads (I could count distinct read_b), while mem_extmm records
  collapsed region relationships.

❯ Listen, listen, listen clearly, first of all we'll clearly clarify two        
  things. In option A, we are not taking anything from archive. So one assembly 
  from that, is part, we are not doing correctly, if I'm not wrong. But rather  
  what we are doing is in the compression time itself we are doing this, so     
  that it can be done. What is it in option A? And what is option A novelty?    

● Clear answer, both parts.

  What A actually does

  Step by step, inside one process:

  1. Encoder reads the FASTQ once, packs reads 2-bit, builds the pseudogenome —
     for compression
  2. CAPS_CALL=1 invokes the caller in that same process
  3. Caller builds a k-mer graph from the reads (the 2-bit packed store already
     in RAM)
  4. Finds bubbles in that graph, filters by read support, emits VCF

  You're right: A does not use the assembly. The pseudogenome, the contigs, the
  12.6 M placements — none of them determine a call. The contigs supply one
  boolean (diploid yes/no) and the placements print a stderr histogram. The
  calling runs off the reads, exactly like DiscoSNP.

  So "we built an assembly and called from it" is not what A does. That was the
  framing I had to withdraw.

  What A's novelty actually is

  It's the single pass — and that part is real.

  SPRING + DiscoSNP:   read FASTQ → compress
                       read FASTQ AGAIN → index → call     (two passes, two
  tools)

  A:                   read FASTQ ONCE → compress + call   (one pass, one tool)

  The reads are parsed once, packed once, and the caller consumes that in-memory
  2-bit store. No re-parse, no second index, no intermediate FASTQ, no temp
  files. One command produces both a lossless archive and a VCF.

  That is a genuine engineering claim, and no competitor can make it: PgRC2 and
  SPRING have no caller at all; DiscoSNP has no archive. Doing both in one pass
  is the thing that's ours.

  But be honest about its limits

  Three things it is not:

  - Not an algorithmic novelty. The bubble-finding is DiscoSNP's method,
    faithfully ported.
  - Not a speed win. A's caller is 106 s; DiscoSNP is 75.7 s. We're slower, so
    "one pass" doesn't buy time — it buys not needing a second tool.
  - Not the source of our F1 edge. 0.8766 vs 0.847 comes from counting k-mers to
    depth 2 instead of 3 — a parameter, not the architecture.

  So the defensible sentence

  ▎ One pass over the FASTQ produces both a lossless archive and reference-free 
  ▎ het-SNV calls at F1 0.8766 (vs DiscoSNP++ 0.847), with the caller consuming 
  ▎ the compressor's own packed read store rather than re-reading or re-indexing
  ▎ the input.

  Everything in that sentence is measured. It claims integration, not a new
  calling algorithm — and it does not claim the archive produces the calls,
  because it doesn't.

● E — final status.

  What it is

  Reading variant candidates straight out of the mismatch records the compressor
  stores to make the archive decodable. No graph, no assembly, no pass over the
  reads.

  The numbers

  candidates      2,518,219        cost  218,555 B  (+0.038% of archive)
  recall             0.9009        ← HIGHER than A's 0.8268
  precision          0.036 raw  /  0.779 at tightest filter
  best F1 alone      0.4909        ← vs A's 0.8766
  rescues            5,578 of A's 7,720 misses (72.3%)
  union with A       0.8739        ← below A, so not usable

  Why it fails — settled today, not guessed

  E has no allele evidence, at any level. I built the fix to check, and it
  refuted itself in one run:

  - the pseudogenome has no read pileup — the two haplotypes are stitched to
    different places
  - MEM references have no region pileup either — they tile the pg, so coverage
    ≡ 1 (measured: 612,053 refs over 93 Mbp, VAF=1.0 on 932,236 of 932,990
    records)

  Its records are region-level ("this region differs from that one here"). A
  variant caller needs read-level counts at one locus. That quantity does not
  exist in E's data and cannot be derived from it.

  That's why D could be rescued by the allele-fraction fix (it records
  individual rejected reads, so I could count distinct ones) and E cannot.

  Verdict

  E is not a method. It is a finding. It cannot be Claim 2, and claiming it
  would not survive the first reviewer who runs the precision number.

  But it is the highest-novelty thing in the project, and it's true:

  ▎ A pseudogenome compressor's back-reference mismatch records already contain 
  ▎ 90% of a sample's heterozygous SNVs — including 72% of those a de Bruijn 
  ▎ bubble caller structurally cannot reach — at ~1 byte per candidate, in bytes
  ▎ the archive stores for decodability. They are not separable into calls, 
  ▎ because the encoding is region-level and retains no per-read allele counts.

  That paragraph goes in Discussion. It is defensible, it's measured, nobody has
  reported it, and it explains a real property of pseudogenome compression.
  Both halves matter — the positive finding and the reason it stops there.

  Claim 2 ships as A.

● Lever 3 is blocked, and the code states why in terms that settle it:

  ▎ *"k-mer counts cannot see this distinction by construction: the collapsed 
  ▎ copies are identical in k-mer space, which is why they collapsed. Placement 
  ▎ is the only signal that separates them."*

  The coherence pass builds a probe map of bubble k-mers and then scans actual 
  reads to find which reads carry them, using their placements and quality
  bitmaps to separate a true het site from a repeat collapse. That cannot be
  sourced from kc — the pass exists precisely because k-mer counts are blind to
  it.

  So "skip decoding the reads entirely" is not achievable without changing 
  results. The 10× cheaper pg-derived k-mer build would produce kc, but the
  reads would still be needed for coherence. I'm recording that as refuted
  rather than leaving it as an open promise:

● You're right to push — my reason was wrong. Two corrections from re-reading:

  1. Placement dispersion is instrumentation, not a filter (EXCL is opt-in via
     CAPS_DBG_EXCL, off by default). So "placement is the only signal" cannot be
     the justification — it doesn't gate anything.
  2. The code says the opposite of what I claimed about k-mer counts:

  ▎ "a canonical k-mer's count in kc IS the number of reads containing it, so 
  ▎ walking the path and taking the minimum gives per-path read support 
  ▎ directly"

  So kc can supply per-path read support (min1/min2). My "k-mer counts provably
  can't substitute" was wrong.

  The real blocker is different — and I found it in the scan loop:

  if ((qi >> 3) < qs.size() && !((qs[qi >> 3] >> (qi & 7)) & 1)) continue;

  The coherence pass counts quality-filtered read support — it skips reads whose
  base at that position is below Q20. kc carries no quality, so it cannot
  reproduce that count. That is why reads are needed, and it also explains why
  the 35 s quality decode is unavoidable on this path.

  Let me check the literature the user asked about:

● Web Search("DiscoSNP kissreads2 read mapping back to bubbles quality filtering
            necessary variant calling k-mer coverage substitute")
  ⎿  Did 1 search in 7s

● Verified — my conclusion was right, my reason was wrong, and the check found a
  new opportunity.

  Conclusion holds, and the literature confirms it: DiscoSNP++ itself runs
  kissreads2, which "maps back the reads... in order to determine the read 
  coverage per allele". Read-scanning is inherent to this method family — nobody
  avoids it. Our coherence pass is our version of that same step.

  But my reason was wrong on both counts:
  - placement dispersion is instrumentation (EXCL off by default), so it gates
    nothing
  - the code explicitly says kc can give per-path read support (min1/min2) — the
    opposite of what I claimed

  The real blocker is quality filtering — the scan skips reads whose base is
  below Q20, and kc carries no quality.

  And that exposes a lever I'd otherwise have missed. Our code comments claim we
  avoid kissreads2 because kc supplies support directly — yet the coherence
  pass scans reads anyway, purely for the quality filter. If quality isn't
  load-bearing, we can skip the 35.25 s quality decode entirely. That's testable
  in one run:

● Found the last big lever. The quality decode is a serial loop over independent
  blocks — each block carries its own blen/bcnt/qmin, is fqz_decompress-ed
  independently, and is written in order. Nothing crosses block boundaries.

  the caller, the output isn't even needed as text — it's reduced to one bit per
  base. So: parse the index, decompress blocks in parallel, and emit the Q20 
  bitmap directly, skipping the 1.86 GB text entirely:

● Now I can see the real structure. Two things stand out immediately:

  1. RAM peak is 5.95 GB but [DBG-RSS] shows only ~6.0 GB at the probe — so kc
     (2.1 GB) plus the reads are both resident simultaneously.
  2. The traversal calls succs() once per node per orientation — 281 M times
     over 140.7 M nodes.

  Let me look at what succs actually costs:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Found the deep inefficiency. succs does 4 independent kc_find binary searches
  over a 140.7 M-entry table. Each is ~27 random memory probes. That's the
  traversal's entire cost:

  140.7M nodes × 2 orientations × 4 probes × ~27 hops ≈ 30 billion random
  accesses

  But the four keys are (fwd<<2)|b for b∈{0,1,2,3} — they differ only in the 
  last 2 bits before canonicalization. Let me verify whether they land near each
  other:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● canon31 scatters the four keys (each may flip to its reverse complement), so
  they don't cluster — the four searches are genuinely independent random walks.
  But that's exactly what makes them prefetchable: all four keys are known
  before any search begins, so the four dependent chains can be interleaved
  instead of run back-to-back.

  Let me verify the memory-boundness rather than assume it:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● The model predicts 113 s of pure memory latency against an observed 53.49 s
  traversal — so roughly half the probes are already being served from cache or
  eliminated by the cnt < MINC early-exit. Same order of magnitude, which
  confirms the traversal is latency-bound, not compute-bound.

  That makes software prefetch the right lever: issue all four canon31 keys'
  first probes together so their latencies overlap instead of serialize.

  But my own memory warns me here — "a filter that wins in a latency-bound loop 
  LOSES in a bandwidth-bound one" — so let me check which regime this is before
  writing code:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Measured in isolation: 1.52× on the exact access pattern, on a table the same
  shape and size as kc. That's the confirmation I needed — it's latency-bound,
  and interleaving the four probes overlaps the misses.

  If that transfers, the traversal goes 53.5 s → ~35 s. Implementing it in

✻ Churned for 1m 42s · done Sunday 7:39 PM

❯  which trades RAM for I/O that means in single lime                           

● In one line: you'd read the k-mer graph off disk instead of holding it in RAM 
  — so RAM drops to ~4 GB, but every graph lookup becomes a disk seek instead of
  a memory access.

  Why that's a bad trade for us specifically: the bubble traversal does 1.1 
  billion probes into kc. In RAM those cost ~80 ns each. From disk, even NVMe is
  ~10 µs — that's 100× slower per probe, and the traversal (48 s today) would
  become hours.

  DiscoSNP gets away with it because GATB's structure is a Bloom-filter-backed
  cascading index that answers "is this k-mer present?" without touching disk
  most of the time — it's a different data structure, not the same one paged
  out. Matching that means replacing kc with a probabilistic index, which
  changes what the caller can ask (no exact counts, and we use counts for MINC,
  H, and per-path support).

  So the honest position: 6.21 GB (Option 0) is close to our floor given we keep
  exact counts on 2.33× more k-mers than DiscoSNP. The 10.25 GB indel path is
  the one with genuine slack — the 4 GB seed-index waste I just fixed is real,
  not architectural.

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Now I have the complete picture. Two shared writes, both order-dependent:

  auto& pr_ = pairs_[{rc_, ac}];                 // first-pair-wins
  if (pr_.n == 0) { pr_.rp = rp; ... }  ++pr_.n;

  auto& a = im[make_tuple(rc_, bub.apos, ...)];  // accumulator
  a.anchors++; a.altcid = ac; a.altpos = ap;     // LAST write wins

  pairs_ keeps the first; im overwrites altcid/altpos so it keeps the last. Both
  are order-sensitive — a naive #pragma omp would silently change results,
  which is precisely the failure the stable_sort comment documents.

  The safe design: each kidx run is independent, so parallelize over runs into
  per-thread maps, then merge in deterministic run order — replaying first-wins
  and last-wins exactly.

  pick min/max explicitly.

● Running. All three items are now built and under test in one run:

  1. indel_pass parallelization — threads over independent kidx anchor runs,
  per-thread maps, merge after. CAPS_INDEL_SERIAL=1 restores serial.

  2. kidx build + sort — this one needed real care. A naive parallel build
  concatenating per-thread buffers would break the insertion order that "first
  pair wins" depends on. Instead: count per contig → prefix-sum → fill by index,
  so the array is byte-identical to the serial push_back order by construction,
  not by luck. Sort uses __gnu_parallel::stable_sort, preserving the stability
  the code says is load-bearing.

  3. Seed-index exact reserve — count kept entries first (the 64-cap makes
  outputs smaller than flat), then reserve exactly, plus shrink_to_fit on flat.

  The gate: VCF compared as a sorted content set, not bytes — because I
  established earlier today that this caller is nondeterministic in contig
  numbering, so byte comparison would report a false failure. Plus both F1
  scores against the 0.5916 / 0.8488 baseline.

  What I expect: if the merge's order-dependence bites, content will differ and
  F1 will move slightly. That's the known weakness I documented rather than
  papered over — and the fix is already specified (carry a per-key run index,
  take min for pairs_ first-wins and max for im last-wins). I'd rather discover
  that from the data than assume it away.

● Still running, and CPU 482% tells the story: it IS parallel, but only ~4.8 
  cores of 12 are busy.

  Why it's taking this long: indel_pass began at ~654 s, we're at 1,847 s, so
  it's ~1,193 s in — already past the 1,153 s serial baseline. So the 
  parallelization is not delivering a speedup, despite genuinely running on
  multiple threads.

  The cause is visible in the number I logged: 86,487,848 anchor runs. That's
  86.5 M loop iterations where the vast majority do nothing — most runs have occ
  < 2 and exit immediately. With schedule(dynamic, 64), that's ~1.35 M
  scheduling handoffs for near-zero work each, and the per-thread std::map
  writes add allocation contention. Classic case of parallelizing at the wrong
  granularity: I threaded the outer loop over runs when the work lives in the
  rare runs with many occurrences.

  The fix is straightforward once the baseline confirms it — filter to the runs
  that actually do work (2 <= occ.size() <= MAXOCC) before parallelizing, so
  threads only receive real work. That turns 86.5 M trivial tasks into a much
  smaller set of substantial ones.

  I'm letting it finish because I need the content check — if the output content
  differs from baseline, that's a separate bug to fix regardless of speed, and
  killing the run now would leave both questions open. ~5 more minutes.

● There it is — the code as written will NOT work.

  read_pos, read_rc, read_clip empty. That's fine for DBG_ONLY (bubbles don't
  use them), but build_substrate needs them to place reads onto contigs.

  With empty placement arrays, build_substrate would produce a substrate with no
  reads mapped — and the indel pass would emit nothing or garbage, silently.
  Exactly the failure mode I warned about, and it would have looked like "indels
  don't work from the archive" rather than "I didn't supply the inputs."

  Two further problems visible from Option 0's log:

  - export gives 2 contigs (pg_main, pg_second), not the 451,760 the in-memory
    path passes. build_substrate collapsing 2 giant contigs is not the same
    operation at all.
  - The placements would have to come from pos_abs — which is in the archive
    (Claim 3's coverage uses it), so the data exists, but nothing wires it into
    CallData.

  So the honest answer to your question changes: not a one-flag fix. The flag
  was necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The archive has the information
  (pos_abs, pos_strand, read lengths), but capsule_decode never reconstructs
  read_cid/read_pos from it, and export doesn't emit per-contig sequences.

  Good thing you said read the code first — running it would have produced a
  plausible-looking empty result and cost 20 minutes to learn less.

  What I built

  The gap: the archive had no way to give the caller read placements, so
  build_substrate would have placed zero reads and the indel pass would have
  emitted nothing — silently.

  Three pieces:

  1. contig_spans stream (encoder) — the chain boundaries. This was the
     genuinely missing information: the decoder rebuilds pg perfectly but never
     sees where one chain ended and the next began, so it cannot be recomputed.
     ~451k spans, delta-coded. Gated on CAPS_CALL, so plain archives stay
     byte-identical.
  2. Per-contig export (decoder) — emits the ~451k real contigs instead of 2
     concatenated records. Handing build_substrate 2 giant records is a
     different operation entirely.
  3. Placement reconstruction (decoder) — pos_abs + pos_strand + spans →
     read_cid/read_pos/read_rc, via binary search into the span table.

  Two traps I hit while writing it

  pos_abs is per-UNIQUE read; the caller indexes per-ORIGINAL. They differ by
  duplicates — the same conflation undercounted coverage 20% on E. coli. Handled
  via orig2uid expansion.

  read_clip has no archive source. The encoder derives it during placement;
  there's no stream. I left it zero and said so in the code, rather than quietly
  assuming it doesn't matter. This is the most likely reason the first 
  comparison won't match — and the VCF diff will tell us.

  What a run would cost

  - Subset (4M reads): ~8 min — answers "does it work, does it place reads, does
    it emit indels"
  - Full chr20: ~30 min — answers "is F1 exactly 0.5916"

  Subset first. Say go.

● In short:

  opt-in.

  T3, T4 and Claim 3, and false for T5, T5.2, T5.3 — those need the FASTQ.

  The only difference: which reads carry their placement forward vs get 
  re-placed. A carries 1,749,455 forward; B carries 1,689,820 — because B
  reconstructs placements from pos_abs at unique-read granularity, while A has
  the encoder's live per-read state. The re-placement step recovers them (totals
  match at ~3.76 M), but a read re-placed by mismatch-tolerant search can land
  a base or two differently than one carried forward.

  read; duplicates share one entry. That's inherent to the format, not something
  I got wrong.

  records differ (0.21%), all in the indel channel.
